articles.title: PHP2Shell: Your Code Was Fine, The Engine Was Not

articles.body_html:
Hello, I'm Maneshwar, and I'm building LiveReview — a blast-radius aware AI code review built for your business-critical systems. Star us to help devs discover the project, give it a try, and share your feedback to help improve the product.

Imagine you do everything right.

You validate your inputs. You use prepared statements. You escape your output. You have a linter, a code review process, and a slightly smug Slack channel called #security-wins.

Then someone sends your server one weird HTTP request, and it runs their code instead of yours.

Not because of anything you wrote.

Because of something PHP did while cleaning up after itself.

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project shipped a security release for two critical bugs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619.

The internet has already nicknamed the pair PHP2Shell, which is a great name and a terrible Wednesday.

Let's walk through what actually broke, why it is a bigger deal than "yet another CVE", and also where the scary headlines are a little ahead of the facts.

Why this one is different

PHP is not a niche language. W3Techs says 69.3% of websites whose server-side language it can identify run PHP.

WordPress, Laravel, Drupal, Magento, that one invoice portal from 2014 that nobody dares touch.

Most PHP vulnerabilities live in an application or a plugin. You patch the plugin, you move on.

These two live in the engine.

The engine is the thing underneath your code. It is the C program that parses your PHP, allocates your memory, and tears down after every request.

You can write the most boring, correct PHP of your life, and the floor below it can still have a hole in it.

[DIAGRAM PLACEHOLDER] the stack, bottom to top: the web server (Apache or nginx), the SAPI (mod_php or PHP-FPM), the PHP engine, then your application code on top. Highlight the engine layer in red with the caption "both bugs live here, below everything you wrote". Show that an attacker's request has to pass through the engine before your code even sees it.

Both bugs are about the same unglamorous thing: memory management around a request that goes wrong.

To see why, you need to know how PHP spends its life.

PHP's life is one request long

PHP's model is famously "shared nothing".

A request comes in, PHP sets up a fresh little world for it, runs your script, then throws the whole world away.

The worker process survives, but the request's state is supposed to die with the request.

That is why PHP is so forgiving. Leak some memory in a script? Nobody cares, the request ends and the memory gets reclaimed.

Here is the happy path:

flowchart LR
    A([Request arrives]):::start --> B[Request startup<br/>build per-request state]:::engine
    B --> C[Run your script]:::app
    C --> D[Request shutdown<br/>cleanup and free]:::engine
    D --> E([Worker waits for the next request]):::start
    E --> A

    classDef start fill:#e9ecef,stroke:#6c757d,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef engine fill:#9d8cff,stroke:#5b4bcc,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef app fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a

Notice that the purple boxes, startup and shutdown, are the engine's job.

Your code only owns the teal one in the middle.

Both vulnerabilities are about what happens when something goes wrong between those purple boxes, and the engine's cleanup code assumes a state that no longer holds.

PHP has a hard ceiling on how much memory one request may use, memory_limit. Hit it, and PHP gives up on the request on the spot.

"Gives up on the spot" is where the trouble starts.

Bug 1: cleaning up a house that was never built

CVE-2026-109618, the out-of-memory one.

Here is the scenario, paraphrasing the PHP Foundation's write-up and Rapid7's analysis.

PHP is in the middle of request startup. It is building that per-request state, piece by piece.

A memory allocation fails. PHP abandons the request abruptly.

But the state is only half built. Some fields are set, some are whatever bytes happened to be sitting in that memory.

Then the cleanup code runs, and it does what cleanup code does: it trusts the state it is handed.

It follows pointers that were never initialized. It frees things that were never allocated. It treats garbage as a structure.

The mental model I like: a demolition crew is sent to tear down a building.

The building was never finished, and the blueprint is a napkin with random scribbles on it.

The crew follows the napkin anyway, and demolishes whatever the scribbles point at.

Here is the shape of the bug as a deliberately simplified sketch. This is not PHP's real source, just the pattern:

// simplified illustration of the bug class, not actual PHP code
int request_startup(request *r) {
    r->headers = alloc_table();     // ok
    r->uploads = alloc_table();     // out of memory! bail out...
    if (!r->uploads) return FAILURE;
    r->hooks   = alloc_table();     // never reached, r->hooks is junk
    return SUCCESS;
}

void request_shutdown(request *r) {
    free_table(r->headers);
    free_table(r->uploads);
    free_table(r->hooks);           // frees a pointer nobody ever set
}

The mistake is not in either function alone. It is in the assumption that shutdown only ever runs on a fully started request.

Now here is the part that makes this one nasty.

How do you make a server run out of memory on purpose? You do not need to hack anything, you just ask nicely and badly.

Rapid7 notes that crafted multipart requests can exhaust memory even when their overall size looks like it fits inside the configured limits.

And on Apache with mod_php, the demonstrated attack happens before any of your application code runs.

That is the whole reason the "zero authentication" line is true. There is no login to bypass. Your code never got the chance to say no.

Memory corruption you can trigger with a request, in a place your app cannot guard, is how you end up with "9.2 critical" in a headline.

Bug 2: the ghost of requests past

CVE-2026-109619, the stale state one.

Same family, different flavour.

Remember that a worker process handles request after request. Some bookkeeping state is global to the worker, and is supposed to be reset between requests.

Now picture this sequence:

sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Request A
    participant W as PHP worker
    participant B as Request B
    A->>W: runs, global state points at memory M
    W->>W: fatal error interrupts cleanup
    W-->>W: M is freed, but the pointer to M is not cleared
    B->>W: arrives on the same worker
    W->>W: reads the old pointer before init resets it
    Note over W: use-after-free: B is reading memory it does not own

A fatal error, like running out of memory or a timeout, can interrupt the cleanup in the middle.

The memory gets freed, but a pointer to it survives. The next request lands on the same worker, and something reads that pointer before normal initialization has a chance to wipe it.

That is a classic use-after-free. The name is the best part, because the thing you are using after it is free is not free at all, it is very expensive.

Think of a hotel room that was demolished but the key card still opens the door.

Whoever is standing there next gets to decide what is inside.

Rapid7 describes two concrete paths to reach it.

One is the PHP 8.5 fatal error backtrace feature, which is on by default and was confirmed on mod_php. The other is a session upload progress path that works on PHP-FPM, and needs an application operation to leave state behind first.

Note the pattern. Neither bug is about a missing bounds check in some parser. They are both about error paths.

The happy path of PHP has been tested for decades. The path where a request dies at the worst possible moment is the one that gets less love.

So can anyone hack 70% of the internet?

Short answer: no, and it is worth being precise, because the headline version of this story sells more than it delivers.

What is solid:

Both bugs are real and rated 9.2 (CVSS 4.0). Both can lead to code execution as the web worker's user, with no authentication.

RCE was demonstrated by researchers, against real setups, not just crashes.

mod_php is the highest risk. Rapid7 notes that for the OOM bug, mod_php runs cleanup even when startup failed. PHP-FPM kills the worker when startup fails, which blocks that specific sequence.

What is more nuanced:

"Any PHP server" is too strong. Rapid7 reviewed multiple public proof of concepts, and each one works only for a specific combination of OS, PHP version and web server. None is broadly reliable yet.

The attack complexity is rated High. Memory corruption exploits are fiddly. That is a speed bump, not a wall.

Reports of exploitation are mixed. watchTowr says it has seen exploitation in the wild through its honeypots, while Rapid7 has seen attempts but not confirmed in-the-wild compromise.

Whichever way that lands, Rapid7 also warns that a more portable technique could show up quickly.

And the exposed surface is not small. Palo Alto's Unit 42 brief cites telemetry that counts over 22 million potentially vulnerable internet-facing instances. That is a vendor number, so season to taste, but it is the right order of magnitude for "a lot".

If I had to summarize it: not the end of the web, but also not a drill.

The part that is actually uncomfortable

Here is the story behind the patch, and it is the most human part of the whole thing.

flowchart LR
    A[2024<br/>Quarkslab audit,<br/>first signs of the OOM issue]:::early --> B[Fix stalls<br/>competing patches,<br/>each with trade-offs]:::slow
    B --> C[Aug 2026<br/>Calif, OpenAI and Wiz<br/>report it, RCE shown]:::report
    C --> D[Oct 20<br/>CVE IDs leak<br/>2 days early]:::bad
    D --> E[Oct 21<br/>Chainguard images<br/>break the embargo]:::bad
    E --> F[Oct 21, 14:00 UTC<br/>patched releases ship]:::good

    classDef early fill:#6ea8ff,stroke:#3a6fcc,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef slow fill:#f4d35e,stroke:#b8991f,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef report fill:#9d8cff,stroke:#5b4bcc,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef bad fill:#ff9a5c,stroke:#cc6a2a,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef good fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a

Per the PHP Foundation, an external audit by Quarkslab back in 2024 led a core developer to spot the first signs of the OOM problem while fixing something else.

No exploit path was known at the time.

Then the fix stalled. Competing patches each had a cost: breaking compatibility, opening new denial of service angles, or touching lots of third-party extensions.

The Foundation's own words are refreshingly blunt: the delay was "a structural failure, caused by both the security team's decision process and its lack of resources."

Then in August 2026 the bug was reported again, with a working unconditional RCE. The CVE IDs leaked online before the release. The embargo then cracked a second time when a vendor published images that already contained the fix.

I find this oddly reassuring and deeply annoying at the same time.

Reassuring, because an open source project wrote that sentence about itself in public, and is changing its process: majority decisions, an ecosystem security team, more staff.

Annoying, because "everyone who maintains critical infrastructure is under-resourced" is not a new lesson, and PHP is carrying a very large share of the web on it.

The AI angle, and where I would push back

A lot of the commentary around this release points at one thing: AI changes who can exploit this.

The argument goes like this. Turning a subtle memory corruption bug into a working attack used to need rare skills. Now somebody with a laptop and an open-weights model can point an agent at the internet, hand it the advisory and say "go find the ones that are still vulnerable".

I think the direction is right and the details are overstated.

What is right: the cost of going from advisory to attempt is falling fast. The patch itself is a diff. A diff tells a model exactly where to look. And scanning is cheap when the scanner does not get tired.

What is overstated: the hard part of this bug is not finding targets, it is the exploit reliability. Rapid7 says the public PoCs are fragile. Memory corruption is a craft, and models are not magic yet at crafting heap layouts for your particular distro.

And there is a side of the story that gets less airtime: the defenders have the same tools.

The Foundation says it used AI-assisted scanning and validation as part of its security work, with the line that "a person makes every call and works on every patch."

So the realistic summary is not "attackers got superpowers". It is this:

The window between "patch published" and "someone is trying it on your server" is shrinking.

Your patching speed is now a security control, not an IT chore.

What to do about it

Boring answer first: update.

The fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35.

If you are on 8.1 or older, there are no routine upstream releases. Rapid7 notes limited source backports exist for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, so lean on your distribution or an LTS vendor, or finally take the upgrade you have been postponing since 2022.

Two gotchas people will trip on:

A patched package on disk is not a patched process in memory. Running workers keep the old code until they restart. Qualys specifically calls this out, so restart or gracefully reload your PHP services after upgrading.

Containers do not save you from stale base images. If your image was built last week, it is still carrying last week's PHP.

Quick check:

php -v                       # compare against 8.5.12 / 8.4.27 / 8.3.36 / 8.2.35

# then make sure the running workers are the new ones
sudo systemctl reload php8.3-fpm     # or: apachectl graceful

If you truly cannot patch yet, the advisories list temporary mitigations. They reduce exposure, they do not fix it:

; php.ini or FPM pool config, NOT ini_set() or .user.ini (too late for these)
session.upload_progress.enabled = 0   ; closes the known session path
fatal_error_backtraces = 0            ; PHP 8.5 only
post_max_size = 8M                    ; and cap multipart size at the frontend too

You will see memory_limit=-1 suggested too, and here is where I have to confess the Roll Safe meme is doing real work:

It genuinely appears in the advisory guidance, set administratively so apps cannot override it. But Rapid7 is clear that an allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path, so it narrows the window and does not close it.

Also, a server with no memory limit has its own personality. It is called "an outage".

And two things not to reach for. Rapid7 warns that RLIMIT_AS and RLIMIT_DATA can themselves trigger the vulnerable allocation failure path, and container or cgroup memory limits are an incomplete answer and can kill the whole worker pool.

Do not hide the evidence either. Silencing errors with display_errors or @ does not prevent stale state from being read, and a quiet log is not proof you are fine.

Here is the whole decision as a flowchart, for the person who has a patch window and a manager:

flowchart TD
    A([Do you run PHP on a web server?]):::start --> B{Is it on 8.2.35, 8.3.36,<br/>8.4.27 or 8.5.12 or newer?}:::decision
    B -- yes --> C{Did you restart or reload<br/>workers after upgrading?}:::decision
    C -- yes --> D([You are patched. Go touch grass.]):::good
    C -- no --> E[Restart workers now]:::action
    B -- no --> F{Is it 8.1 or older?}:::decision
    F -- yes --> G[Distro or LTS backport,<br/>or plan the upgrade]:::action
    F -- no --> H[Upgrade to a fixed release]:::action
    G --> I[Apply interim mitigations<br/>until it lands]:::warn
    H --> E

    classDef decision fill:#f4d35e,stroke:#b8991f,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef start fill:#e9ecef,stroke:#6c757d,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef good fill:#5ee6c8,stroke:#1f9c86,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef action fill:#6ea8ff,stroke:#3a6fcc,color:#1a1a1a
    classDef warn fill:#ff9a5c,stroke:#cc6a2a,color:#1a1a1a

The thing worth taking away

The patch is the urgent lesson. The durable one is quieter.

Your security posture includes layers you did not write and never read.

Your code can be perfect and the runtime under it can still ship a bug that was first noticed two years ago.

That is not a reason to panic about PHP specifically. Every runtime has error paths nobody loves, and the next bug of this kind will be in a different one.

It is a reason to treat runtime and base image updates as first class work, to know which version is actually running in production, and to keep the gap between "advisory" and "deployed" as small as you can.

Cleanup code, it turns out, is also code.

Maybe even the code most worth reviewing.


Your team's attention is limited, and the deluge of AI-generated code is making it harder to keep production secure and reliable without slowing you down.

articles.title: "Build in Public" Is Everywhere. Does It Actually Get You Customers? 🤔

articles.body_html:
What founders report, what that evidence can't prove, and a four-week experiment you can run on your own product.

In 2023, the founders of Senja, a customer-testimonial tool, noticed how much attention revenue screenshots were getting in the build-in-public community. They gave the makers who focused on milestones a nickname: "milestone men." Then they started sharing losses and context alongside their wins.

They weren't skeptics, though. In the same interview, co-founder Olly said one in four of Senja's paying customers came from Twitter and building in public.

So one practice earned applause for some founders and, by one founder's account, paying customers for another. This article is about the gap between those outcomes. The question isn't whether building in public is good or bad. It's what has to be true between a post getting attention and a stranger paying for your software.

We'll look at what attention metrics can and can't tell you, then three documented accounts: a modest success, a spectacular one, and a failure. Then I'll explain why even those are weaker evidence than they look. Finally, we'll turn the patterns into an experiment small enough for a solo founder to run without losing a quarter.

One phrase, four different activities

"Building in public" gets used for at least four things that behave differently.

  • Progress sharing: changelogs, screenshots, technical decisions. Mostly interesting to people who care about the process.
  • Metrics sharing: revenue, signups, churn. It builds credibility, and as the Senja founders noticed, it can easily turn into a performance.
  • Teaching: posts that solve a reader's problem whether or not they ever buy. This is content marketing under a founder's name.
  • Conversation: asking users for feedback and answering people who have the problem you solve.

This split is my own, not an industry standard. It matters because the activities tend to attract different kinds of attention. Progress and metrics posts often draw people who like following founders. Teaching and conversation tend to draw people with the problem. Those groups sometimes overlap, but often they don't, and the product, audience, and platform all change the picture.

What a like measures

A founder's funnel has more stages than a social feed shows. Treat this table as a simplified model, not a strictly linear customer journey:

Stage What you can count What it tells you
Attention Impressions, likes, followers People saw it and reacted. Not proof of buying intent.
Interest Replies and DMs from people who fit your buyer profile, email signups Someone with the problem wants more
Trial Signups, then activated users (these are different things) Someone tried the product, and maybe got value from it
Revenue Paying customers Someone valued it enough to pay
Durability Retention, or repeat purchases for non-subscription products The value held up

Not everyone who sees a post moves to the next stage, and many never do. How big the drop-off is depends on your audience, your offer, and your channel. A post can do brilliantly at the top while adding nothing at the bottom. If your audience is mostly other founders and you sell to dentists, a viral thread is a pleasant event with no commercial consequence. Your mom will be very proud, though. 🦷

There's a complication in the other direction. Influence doesn't always show up as a click. Olly said far more happens in DMs than people assume, especially around launches. Readers who never click a link may still remember your name later. That's an argument for tracking conversations, not just clicks, and for asking new users how they found you. Self-reported attribution is imperfect, but it beats assuming the answer is "direct."

Three accounts, three different lessons

Senja: customers, with caveats. The interview ran in March 2023, when Senja had reached $4,000 in monthly recurring revenue in under a year. Olly reported that one in three signups and one in four paying customers came from Twitter and building in public, and that he spent about seven hours a week on it. Note that those figures combine Twitter and building in public, so they don't isolate the effect of building in public itself. He called it, along with SEO, the best-return marketing work they did. He also listed conditions that cut against the hype. It's easier if you're making a product for other makers, it can take months to generate sales even then, and he wasn't starting from zero, since he already had a small audience from an earlier project.

RB2B: the spectacular case. Adam Robinson's account is the dramatic one. Interviews, including a ProductLed podcast episode, report that he took RB2B, a website-visitor identification product, to $5 million in annual recurring revenue in about 13 months with a tiny team, using LinkedIn heavily for awareness. A Trueframe write-up of his published figures (Trueframe is a content agency, so read it with that in mind) says he attributed about 75% of site traffic to LinkedIn in an October 2025 snapshot. It also notes that his own launch retrospectives disagree on basics, such as 1,600 waitlist members in one telling versus 3,000 free signups in another, and that meme content drew attention from people outside his buyer group. Now look at what surrounds those numbers. He already ran a larger, established company, his LinkedIn audience was made of SaaS operators, and RB2B sells to SaaS operators. That's less "I posted memes and got rich" and more "I posted to the exact people who buy." Treat all of this as his claims, not audited results.

A six-month failure. A founder wrote on Indie Hackers in September 2025 about posting daily updates, sharing the journey on Reddit, and ending up with 43 signups, 2 paying customers, and $18 in monthly revenue. Their own diagnosis was that the people cheering them on were supporters, not people with the problem. It's a single self-reported anecdote, and the post ends by linking the author's product, so weigh it accordingly. It's also as much a story about weak demand and validation as about building in public. Lots of cheering, very little paying.

What these accounts can't tell us

These stories are interesting, but they don't prove that building in public causes customers. Here's why.

First, every account is self-reported. Nobody audited these numbers, and an interview with a founder is a founder describing their own business.

Second, none of them isolates building in public from everything else. Senja credits SEO alongside Twitter. Robinson had an existing company and a reputation among his buyers. The failed project may simply have lacked a real problem to solve. The strategy might be the cause, a contributor, or just a companion to something else, and a story told after the fact can't separate those.

Third, we mostly hear from the visible. Founders who posted for a year, got nothing, and moved on rarely write retrospectives. That's my inference, not a measured fact. I couldn't find a controlled comparison of founders who build in public and similar founders who don't. If you see a precise "founders who build in public grow X times faster" statistic, ask where the denominator came from.

The three cases don't produce the same outcome, but they share a thread. Where the strategy visibly worked, the audience was close to the buyer. That's suggestive, not conclusive.

When it seems to work, and when it probably doesn't

Treat these as hypotheses consistent with the accounts above, not proven rules.

Audience overlap. Senja said building in public is easier for a product aimed at makers, and Robinson's audience matched his buyers. The failed project's audience was supporters. If your customers aren't on the platforms where founders talk to each other, you may grow a friendly audience that's useless to your revenue.

Content a buyer would value. Senja's "milestone men" and engagement from people who were never going to buy teach the same lesson from two directions: attention from the wrong people, or about the wrong thing, doesn't convert. A revenue screenshot can show that a business exists. On its own, it rarely shows a buyer that you'll solve their problem.

A route from reading to trying. A free tier, a waitlist, and Senja's DM follow-ups all give an interested reader a next step. This one is my inference from the accounts, not something any of them tested. Attention without a path leaves people with nowhere to go.

Time, including yours. Seven hours a week is nearly a full working day for a solo founder. The honest comparison isn't "posting versus nothing." It's posting versus the same hours spent building, or reaching out directly to people who fit your buyer profile.

One more thing the success stories don't dwell on: transparency is a strategic choice, not an obligation to disclose everything. Customer details, security specifics, and anything covered by a contract don't belong in a public update, however good the engagement would be.

A four-week experiment

Four weeks is a proposed starting point, not a proven duration. Senja's experience suggests sales can take months, so this experiment measures leading indicators, not revenue. The question it answers: is public content producing conversations with people who look like buyers?

  1. Baseline (before week 1). Record how many signups you get per week now and where they come from. Note how many hours you can honestly spend. Without a baseline, any result is uninterpretable, and I'm not aware of a defensible benchmark conversion rate to use instead.
  2. Audience. Write one sentence naming who pays you and where they already read or talk. If you can't, you've learned something important before posting a single word.
  3. Hypothesis. Something like "Posting twice a week in [place] will start conversations with at least [N] people who fit my buyer profile." Set N before you start, based on your baseline and your available hours (for example, what the same hours of direct outreach would produce), not after you see the results. Moving the goalposts is a sport, but not this one.
  4. Content. Mix teaching posts that address a buyer's problem, build updates framed around what changed for a user, and replies in existing communities. Treat revenue and milestone screenshots as optional. Log which type of post led to each qualified conversation, so you learn what worked and not just that something did.
  5. Distribution. Pick one or two places where buyers already spend time. Reply and participate more than you broadcast.
  6. Measurement. Leading indicators: replies and DMs from people who fit your buyer profile, and qualified visits to your site. Middle: signups and activation. Lagging: paying customers and retention, which probably won't show up in four weeks, so don't conclude from their absence alone.
  7. Attribution. Use a distinct tracked link per channel and log DMs by hand. Add one free-text "how did you hear about us?" question at signup, and let people name more than one touchpoint, since someone may see a post, come back later, and sign up through a search result. Accept that this undercounts, because readers who see a post and return later will often look like direct traffic.
  8. Review and decision rules. Check in at the end of week two to see whether the routine is sustainable and the content is landing with the right people. At week four, look at the quality of conversations (one qualified chat can beat ten polite likes), whether any turned into trials, how much time you spent, and whether you're reaching the right audience. Then decide whether to continue, change the channel or content, or run another cycle. Don't use four weeks to declare the whole strategy a success or a failure. If attention is high but buyers are absent, that usually points to the wrong venue or topic, not the wrong product. Consider demoting it to an accountability and networking habit if, after two cycles (my suggestion, not a proven threshold), qualified conversations stay near zero.

So, does it get you customers? 🎯

Sometimes. In the documented cases where it did, the audience was already close to the buyer, the content was useful to that buyer, and there was a path from reading to trying. When those conditions are missing, building in public may still help with accountability, feedback, and networking, but its value as a customer-acquisition channel becomes much less certain.

How often it works across all founders, nobody can say from the evidence available. What you can do is test it on your own product, with your own baseline, before spending a year on it.

So here's the question I'd most like to see answered in the comments. If you've built in public for a product whose buyers weren't other builders (dentists, accountants, game studios, anyone), where did your first ten paying customers actually come from, and could you trace any of them back to a public post?

Here is a scenario almost every developer reading this has lived through over the past year.

It is 11:30 PM. You are working on a feature, like adding real-time order tracking to an existing e-commerce service. You open your favorite AI coding assistant (Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, or Antigravity) and type what feels like a sensible prompt:

"Add real-time order tracking using WebSockets and Redis."

You hit enter. The assistant doesn't hesitate. Within three seconds, it starts furiously streaming code.

It writes a WebSocket gateway from scratch and invents an ad-hoc Redis pub/sub wrapper. It drops a global state variable right into your React layout, pulls in a third-party reconnect library you've never heard of, and for good measure, rewrites half of your existing Order model, breaking six unrelated unit tests in the process.

The diff looks like a crime scene.

Imagine an eager junior developer doing this on their first week: rewriting domain models, swapping libraries, and modifying database schemas without asking a single clarifying question. You wouldn't applaud their speed. You would sit them down and have a serious conversation about requirements, architecture boundaries, and scope.

Yet with AI assistants, we've normalized this exact pathology. We treat rapid token output as "productivity," only to spend the next three hours cleaning up broken architectural seams, untangling hidden race conditions, and undoing premature abstractions.

The problem isn't that modern LLMs can't write code. The problem is that they start writing code way too early.

And strangely enough, the best antidote to this problem was published eighty years ago by a Stanford mathematician.

The Root Cause: Autoregressive Myopia

Large Language Models are, by their foundational design, autoregressive greedy token generators. When given a prompt, their training compels them to emit the most probable continuation immediately.

They have no built-in pause button. They don't take a sip of coffee, look at your existing repository structure, and wonder:

  • What domain entities already exist here?
  • What is the SLA for latency and reconnection?
  • What are the sad paths if the Redis broker restarts?
  • Is WebSockets even the right architectural trade-off here, or would Server-Sent Events (SSE) solve this in 50 fewer lines of code?

Instead, they dive headfirst into implementation.

Research in cognitive science identified this trap decades ago. In 1985, UC Berkeley researcher Alan H. Schoenfeld published Mathematical Problem Solving, studying how students and mathematicians tackle tough problems. He discovered that novice problem-solvers spend almost zero time analyzing the problem; they jump straight into calculations, follow an unviable path into a dead end, and burn all their time backtracking.

Experts do the exact opposite. They spend the vast majority of their time analyzing constraints, drawing figures, and discarding bad directions before calculating anything.

Schoenfeld proved that problem-solving strategies fail without what he called metacognitive supervisory control: the conscious ability to halt, assess progress, and refuse to proceed on unverified assumptions.

Modern AI coding agents are the ultimate novices. They possess encyclopedic syntax knowledge, but zero metacognitive control.

Enter George Pólya (1945)

In 1945, Hungarian-American mathematician George Pólya published a compact, 250-page book at Princeton University Press called How to Solve It. It went on to sell over a million copies and was translated into 17 languages.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   GEORGE PÓLYA'S 4-STAGE HEURISTIC (1945)              │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 1. UNDERSTAND THE PROBLEM  ➔  What is the unknown? What are the data?  │
│                               What is the condition? Can it be met?    │
│ 2. DEVISE A PLAN           ➔  Find connections between data & unknown. │
│                               Isolate auxiliary problems. Restate it.  │
│ 3. CARRY OUT THE PLAN      ➔  Check each step. Can you prove that each │
│                               individual step is sound and correct?    │
│ 4. LOOK BACK (EXAMINE)     ➔  Check the result. Derive it differently. │
│                               Promote reusable patterns to memory.     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Pólya wasn't interested in rigid mathematical proofs written after the fact. He was obsessed with the psychology of discovery: how people actually navigate uncertainty. He codified problem-solving into four invariant stages:

  1. Understand the Problem: Deconstruct The Unknown (what are we trying to produce?), The Data (what inputs and state exist?), and The Condition (what constraints and business rules must hold true?).
  2. Devise a Plan: Find the connection between the data and the unknown. Consider auxiliary problems. Work backwards. Restate the problem.
  3. Carry Out the Plan: Verify each step along the way. Prove correctness as you move forward.
  4. Look Back: Examine the result. Can you derive it more simply? Can you use this method for other problems?

In 1961, AI pioneer Marvin Minsky cited Pólya in his landmark paper Steps Toward Artificial Intelligence, noting: "Everyone should know the work of George Pólya on how to solve problems." In 1982, computer scientist R. Geoff Dromey adapted Pólya's work for algorithmic design in How to Solve It by Computer.

A few months ago, while wrestling with an AI agent that kept hallucinating database columns, the lightbulb went off:

AI agents need George Pólya's discipline far more than human developers do.

Bridging Pólya with Uncle Bob's Clean Architecture

Mathematical heuristics provide the cognitive scaffolding, but software engineering needs concrete physical boundaries.

We paired Pólya's four stages with Robert C. Martin's ("Uncle Bob") Clean Architecture principles: strict dependency inversion, decoupled domain entities, interfaces (ports) separating business logic from infrastructure adapters, and intention-revealing clean code.

The result is Pólya SDLC Coder: an open-source suite of 15 modular agent skills structured across a disciplined 6-phase lifecycle.

Here is how Pólya's 1945 heuristics map directly to modern software craftsmanship across all 15 skills:

George Pólya's Heuristic (1945) Software Craftsmanship Seam Agent Skill Command
"Getting Acquainted" Codebase Reconnaissance & Topography Map /to-ask-help, /to-map & /to-init
"Understanding the Problem" Discovery, PRDs, DTOs & Seam Mapping /to-explore, /to-prd & /to-spec
"Challenging Premises" Socratic Sparring & Concrete A/B Trade-Offs /to-grill-me
"Interrogating the Condition" 5-Axis Assumption Check & 0-100 Readiness Gate /to-clarify
"Devising a Plan" Vertical Tracer Bullets & Plan B Contingencies /to-plan
"The Hesitation Before Calculating" Explicit Human Alignment Gate 🛑 The Mandatory Pause Rule
"Carrying Out the Plan" Clean Code, <25 Line Functions & Micro-TDD /to-code & /to-quick-fix
"Looking Back & Root Cause" 5 SOLID Audit, First-Principles Fix & Diátaxis Docs /to-review, /to-fix & /to-docs
"The Two Golden Questions" Cross-Session Architectural Memory /to-memory

How It Works in Practice

Let's revisit our real-time order tracking feature, but run it through the Pólya workflow.

Step 1: Autonomous Triage (/to-ask-help)

In a brownfield repository, /to-map first scans your directory structure and maintains a living topography map at docs/ARCHITECTURE.md so the agent knows your exact layer boundaries without re-reading a thousand files on every prompt.

Then, instead of throwing a raw feature command at the agent, you run:

/to-ask-help Add real-time order tracking using WebSockets and Redis

The agent doesn't write code. It inspects your repo, locates existing domain models, checks your HTTP framework, and returns a Pólya Triage Card:

+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                         POLYA TRIAGE CARD                             |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| The Unknown   : Real-time WebSocket order tracking stream             |
| The Data      : Order entity, Redis Pub/Sub adapter, React UI hook    |
| The Condition : Sub-100ms latency, automatic reconnection, JWT auth   |
| Seams Found   : Domain (Order), Adapters (RedisStream), UI (Hook)     |
| Recommended   : /to-explore or /to-spec                               |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------+

If the problem space is still wide open, /to-explore runs architectural spikes using Pólya's Inventor's Paradox, and /to-prd frames user stories and explicit non-goals before locking in technical contracts.

Step 2: Socratic Sparring (/to-grill-me)

Before drafting a spec, you put the idea through the sparring partner:

/to-grill-me "Should we use WebSockets or Server-Sent Events (SSE) for order tracking?"

Unlike generic assistants that reply with a 10-paragraph essay saying "Both are great options depending on your needs!", the Pólya sparring skill enforces The 1-Question Rule and The Opinionated Senior Recommendation:

[Option A: Server-Sent Events (SSE)]

Unidirectional stream over standard HTTP/2. Reuses existing auth headers, requires no custom heartbeat/ping-pong machinery, and reconnects automatically via the native browser EventSource API.

[Option B: WebSockets]

Bidirectional full-duplex socket. Requires dedicated connection lifecycle handling, custom JWT handshake validation, and manual heartbeat ping/pong to detect dead TCP sockets.

Senior Recommendation:

I recommend Option A (SSE). Order tracking is 100% server-to-client (the client never pushes coordinate telemetry back through this channel). WebSockets add stateful socket maintenance overhead for a problem that HTTP/2 streaming solves natively.

The One Question: Do you anticipate riders or customers sending real-time messages over this exact stream in V1, or is client-to-server interaction strictly handled by standard REST endpoints?

One sharp question. Real architectural trade-offs. The decision is settled in 30 seconds, saving hours of unnecessary WebSocket plumbing.

Step 3: Vertical Tracer Bullets (/to-plan)

With the trade-offs settled, /to-spec formalizes the data contracts and architectural seams into docs/spec/, flagging any unverified premises with explicit [ASSUMPTION] tags. Before planning can begin, /to-clarify audits the specification across five axes and enforces an objective 0-100 Readiness Gate (anything scoring under 80 blocks the pipeline until ambiguities are resolved).

Once cleared, instead of horizontal slicing (writing all database tables, then all controllers, then all UI), /to-plan devises Vertical Tracer Bullets:

  • Tracer Bullet 1: Domain Event + SSE emitter port + integration mock.
  • Tracer Bullet 2: HTTP endpoint with JWT auth verification.
  • Tracer Bullet 3: Frontend UI subscription hook with connection status badge.
  • Contingency Plan B: Graceful fallback to 5-second polling if HTTP stream drops.

Step 4: 🛑 The Mandatory Pause Rule

Here is the single most critical guardrail in the entire system.

The moment the plan is generated, the agent stops cold. It is strictly forbidden from writing a single line of production code.

It prints:

🛑 MANDATORY GATE: THE PAUSE RULE
The implementation plan is staged at docs/plan/order-tracking-plan.md.
Execution is halted. Awaiting explicit user confirmation before writing code.

This enforces Alan Schoenfeld's supervisory control. You inspect the tracer bullets. If an assumption looks wrong, you fix it in markdown in 10 seconds.

Only when you explicitly type:

"Plan reviewed and approved. Proceed to implementation."

...does the agent move to /to-code.

Step 5: Implementation & Audit (/to-code & /to-review)

During /to-code, the agent is governed by Uncle Bob's Clean Code constraints:

  • Functions must stay under 25 lines.
  • One level of abstraction per function.
  • Intention-revealing naming.
  • Anti-Cheat Floor Guard: Strictly forbidden from using @ts-ignore, skipping tests, or leaving dummy // TODO stubs.
  • Two-Layer Testing: Every tracer bullet must pass fast typechecks (check:fast) and task unit tests (check:task) before the task is marked done.

Finally, /to-review audits the diff against the 5 SOLID principles and 14 defensive security vectors (OWASP, tenant isolation, input sanitization), issuing a definitive release verdict (GO or NO-GO). When approved, /to-docs authors structured documentation based on the Diátaxis framework so your team inherits clean guides alongside clean code.

Before vs. After: What the Code Actually Looks Like

To see the real-world difference, look at what happens at the code level when a courier updates an order's live location to broadcast over our stream.

Without Pólya (The Default AI Spurt):
The AI dumps everything into an ad-hoc controller, mixing raw Redis sockets, direct SQL queries, and unhandled promise rejections:

// The typical AI hallucination: business logic tangled directly with transport
app.post('/api/orders/:id/location', async (req, res) => {
  const redis = new Redis(process.env.REDIS_URL); // New connection on every HTTP request!
  const order = await db.query('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = $1', [req.params.id]);

  if (!order.rows[0]) return res.status(404).send('Not found');

  await db.query('UPDATE orders SET lat = $1, lng = $2 WHERE id = $3', [
    req.body.lat, req.body.lng, req.params.id
  ]);
  redis.publish(`order-stream:${req.params.id}`, JSON.stringify(req.body));
  // No domain validation, zero port abstractions, connection leaks in production
  res.json({ updated: true });
});

With Pólya & Clean Architecture (/to-code):
Because /to-spec established the seams upfront, the agent outputs a decoupled domain port and an intention-revealing use case under 25 lines:

// Clean Architecture: Pure Use Case decoupled from HTTP, SQL, and SSE/Redis transport
export class PublishOrderLocationUseCase {
  constructor(
    private readonly orderRepo: OrderRepositoryPort,
    private readonly streamPublisher: OrderStreamPublisherPort
  ) {}

  async execute(input: UpdateOrderLocationDto): Promise<Result<void, OrderDomainError>> {
    const order = await this.orderRepo.findById(input.orderId);
    if (!order) {
      return Result.fail(new OrderNotFoundError(input.orderId));
    }

    const moveResult = order.recordLocation(input.coordinates);
    if (moveResult.isFailure) {
      return Result.fail(moveResult.error);
    }

    await this.orderRepo.save(order);
    await this.streamPublisher.publish(order.toTrackingEvent());
    return Result.ok();
  }
}

Whether the outer OrderStreamPublisherPort adapter pushes over Server-Sent Events (as chosen during /to-grill-me) or fans out through Redis Pub/Sub, the core domain use case doesn't care. No connection leaks, transport-agnostic domain logic, and 100% mockable unit tests in isolation.

Beyond the Happy Path: Day-2 Engineering Realities

Shipping the initial feature is only half the battle. Most AI workflows fall apart on Day 2 when chat context windows reset, production bugs surface, or you just need a quick config tweak without ceremony.

1. Curing the "AI Amnesia" Trap (/to-memory)

Every developer using AI coding agents knows the frustration of session resets. You spend two hours aligning on an architectural pattern, the context window fills up, you open a new chat, and the agent immediately forgets every single design decision you made.

Pólya SDLC solves this by making session memory durable in memory.instructions.md. When you finish a milestone or settle a complex architectural trade-off, running /to-memory compacts your current findings:

  • Active tracer bullets and their completion status
  • Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) accepted during /to-grill-me
  • Known codebase pitfalls and negative constraints

When you start your next session tomorrow morning, the agent reads this file first. Zero context loss, zero repeating yourself.

2. Bug Fixing Without Whack-A-Mole (/to-fix)

When a defect does occur, default AI behavior is notorious for playing blind whack-a-mole: patching a symptom, introducing two new edge-case failures, and spiraling into nested hacks.

Through /to-fix, the agent is strictly forbidden from blind shotgun patching. Instead, it returns to first principles:

  1. It uses bisection search (O(log n)) to trace and isolate the exact broken architectural seam.
  2. It formulates an automated reproduction test that fails for the exact expected reason first.
  3. It locks in a root-cause remediation plan in docs/bug-reports/ before handing execution over to /to-code.

No guesswork, no hack loops, and no regression cascades.

3. Fast-Track Edits: Pedantry vs. Mastery (/to-quick-fix)

One of George Pólya's most famous quotes from 1945 warns against dogmatism:

"To apply a rule to the letter, rigidly, unquestioningly... is pedantry. To apply a rule with natural ease, with judgment, noticing the cases where it fits... is mastery."

If you need to fix a typo in a config file or tweak a CSS margin on a button, running a full 6-phase SDLC with specifications and Socratic sparring is ridiculous.

For small, routine changes (affecting one or two files), Pólya SDLC provides a fast-track bypass:

/to-quick-fix Fix typo in redis timeout config and increase retry limit to 5

It skips the formal documentation overhead while still upholding typechecks, clean formatting, and atomic git commits.

Trying It Out in Your Codebase

Pólya SDLC Coder is open-source (MIT licensed) and works across any platform supporting agent skills or instruction rules, including Cursor, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Google Antigravity, and ChatGPT Codex.

Quick Setup via npx skills

You don't need to clone large repositories or install heavy npm dependencies. You can install the skills directly using the universal npx skills CLI:

# Option A: Install the lightweight bootstrapper skill
npx skills add GulajavaMinistudio/polya-sdlc-coder/skills/to-init

# Option B: Or install the entire 15-skill suite directly
npx skills add GulajavaMinistudio/polya-sdlc-coder

Then in your AI assistant chat window, simply type:

/to-init setup this project

The bootstrapper will inspect your repository, scaffold .agents/, configure AGENTS.md, and hook up the full 15-skill suite automatically.

(Alternatively, if you prefer shell one-liners, check out the interactive web configurator for macOS, Linux, and Windows.)

Closing Thoughts

AI coding tools are not going away. But the honeymoon phase of "look how fast this LLM can vomit 500 lines of unreviewed code" is ending. Engineering teams are waking up to the maintenance hangover of AI-generated spaghetti.

The secret to building reliable software with AI isn't faster models or larger context windows.

It is having the engineering humility to pause, understand the problem, challenge our premises, and verify the plan before writing the first line of code.

George Pólya figured that out in 1945. It just took us eighty years (and a few million hallucinated tokens) to catch up.

Links & Resources

  • 📐 GitHub Repository: GulajavaMinistudio/polya-sdlc-coder
  • 🌐 Interactive Web Docs & Skill Catalog: gulajavaministudio.github.io/polya-sdlc-coder
  • 📖 The 1945 Origin Story: Why Pólya? (Deep Dive)

Over to You

How are you keeping your AI coding agents from jumping straight into premature spaghetti code? Do you enforce a spec-first workflow, custom instruction files, or manual review gates?

And what is the wildest architectural mess an AI assistant has ever tried to sneak into your codebase? Drop your war stories and workflows in the comments below. I'd love to compare notes!
