articles.title: I Got Tired of Switching Tools While Coding on My Phone, So I Built This
articles.description: Hey everyone!  I made a web framework called Authtics Host, also known as HostJS, and one of the...
articles.body_html:
Hey everyone!

I made a web framework called Authtics Host, also known as HostJS, and one of the things I'm most proud of is its built-in Developer Panel.

The reason I wanted this is pretty simple: I develop stuff on my phone. 💀

When you're developing a website, you need to check logs, investigate requests, see what's happening on the server, and figure out why something isn't working. Switching between tools just to do that gets annoying pretty quickly on a phone.

So I wanted those tools available right inside the framework I'm already using.

That's where the Developer Panel comes in.

What is Authtics Host?

Authtics Host is a web framework inspired by Next.js. It uses TypeScript, TSX, React, and Esbuild, and supports SSR (Server-Side Rendering), SSG (Static Site Generation), CSR (Client-Side Rendering), and SRTWS (Site Rendering Through WebSockets, which is currently in beta).

I'm still working on improving it, but I wanted to share one of its features that has genuinely helped me while developing.

Getting started

First, you'll need Node.js 22.

Install Authtics Host using npm:

npm install @bananacool467/authtics-host@latest

For a basic project, you can use a structure like this:

my-project/
├── index.ts
├── authtics_host.config.ts
└── client/
    ├── public/
    └── pages/
        └── index.tsx

In index.ts, create the app:

import { App } from "@bananacool467/authtics-host";

const app = new App();

Then configure the framework in authtics_host.config.ts:

import { defineConfig } from "@bananacool467/authtics-host";

export default defineConfig({
  port: 8000,
  renderType: "ssr",
  devMode: true,
  autoFile: true,
  autoPage: true,
  autoPageDir: "client/pages",
  autoFileDir: "client/public"
});

Finally, create client/pages/index.tsx:

export default function Index() {
  return (
    <p>Hello, World!</p>
  );
}

Start the project with:

node --experimental-strip-types index.ts

You should get your page, and with development mode enabled, you should also see a clickable Developer Panel at the bottom-right.

So, what's in the Developer Panel?

The panel has nine tabs:

  • Console — View current logs.
  • Route — Check information about the current route.
  • Webpage Info — See information about the current webpage.
  • Network — Check the current ping and inspect fetch requests sent from the client and responses received from the server.
  • Client Info — View the client's user agent, operating system, and FPS.
  • About Host — Check the current Authtics Host version.
  • Server Info — Check server heap usage, CPU usage, request count, connected users, and uptime.
  • Settings — Customize the Developer Panel.
  • Package Security — Your project's security ( Unavailable because it's under development ).

Here's what it looks like:


The panel gives you somewhere to look when you're trying to figure out what's going on with your application, without having to keep switching to a separate tool for every little thing.

For example, if a request isn't behaving the way you expected, you can check the Network tab. If you're trying to figure out what the application is logging, you can check the Console tab.

You also have route and client information available when you need it.

Obviously, this doesn't mean you will never need other debugging tools. It's just convenient to have these features available in the framework itself.

It can do more than inspect things

The Developer Panel also has controls for managing the running app.

Depending on how you've configured access, you can restart or shut down the app and pause or resume incoming users.

That can be useful when you're testing something and need to control what's happening without going off to manage the server separately.

A quick note about developer access

The panel uses something called a DAT (Developer Access Token).

If you configure a DAT in authtics_host.config.ts, you can restrict developer access using a token you specify:

export default defineConfig({
  port: 8000,
  renderType: "ssr",
  devMode: true,
  dat: "YOUR DAT HERE"
});

Replace YOUR DAT HERE with your own token. Don't publish a real token in your source code or share it publicly.

You can also configure an array of DATs if multiple developers need access.

Without a DAT restriction configured, the panel only provides access to the Console and Network tabs. Setting a DAT restriction enables access to the other developer features, including the app management controls.

Since the panel can expose information about your app and provide controls over the server, make sure you configure access appropriately before deploying anything publicly. You can also turn the panel off by setting devMode to false.

Why I built it this way

This is the part that matters most to me.

I didn't build the Developer Panel just to have another feature to list in a README. I built it because I actually use it.

When you're coding on a phone, little inconveniences add up. Having the console, network information, client details, and server information in one place means I don't have to keep interrupting my workflow to go somewhere else just to investigate what's happening.

And that's really the goal of Authtics Host: make web development more convenient, especially for people working from mobile devices.

I'm not saying this will magically make every developer faster, or that everyone needs another framework. I built something that solves a problem I personally ran into, and the Developer Panel has helped me with my own work.

That's a pretty good reason for me to keep improving it.

Try it out

Authtics Host is available on npm:

https://www.npmjs.com/package/@bananacool467/authtics-host

The package includes more than just the Developer Panel, so check out the README for the other framework features and configuration options.

If you try it, I'd genuinely like to hear what works for you and what needs improvement. Feedback is useful, especially while the project is still evolving.

Thanks for reading!

articles.title: Your Custom Hooks Tear in React 18. `useSyncExternalStore` Fixes It.
articles.description: A useState + useEffect hook that subscribes to window size, localStorage, or a WebSocket looks fine until React 18's concurrent rendering shows two parts of your UI two different values at once. useSyncExternalStore is the hook built to stop that.
articles.body_html:
The header says "You're offline." Three pixels below it, the save button is still clickable, sending requests like nothing's wrong. Same navigator.onLine value. Same render. Two different answers on screen at the same time.

You didn't write a new bug. You wrote the hook everyone writes.

function useOnlineStatus() {
  const [online, setOnline] = useState(navigator.onLine);

  useEffect(() => {
    const update = () => setOnline(navigator.onLine);
    window.addEventListener('online', update);
    window.addEventListener('offline', update);
    return () => {
      window.removeEventListener('online', update);
      window.removeEventListener('offline', update);
    };
  }, []);

  return online;
}

It worked in every app you shipped before React 18. Then a teammate wraps a route transition in startTransition to keep the UI responsive, two components that both call useOnlineStatus() briefly disagree, and you spend an afternoon adding console.log statements to a bug that reproduces maybe one time in fifteen.

Why a perfectly normal hook starts lying

useState + useEffect assumes something React 18 no longer guarantees: that once a component commits, it stays committed until the next explicit update, and that every component re-renders from the same world.

Concurrent rendering breaks that assumption on purpose. React can start rendering a tree, pause partway through to handle something more urgent — a keystroke, a transition — and resume later. If the external value your hook reads (navigator.onLine, window.innerWidth, a value in localStorage, a WebSocket payload) changes in that gap, some components finish rendering with the old value and some with the new one. Nothing crashes. You just get a UI where two places disagree about one fact, for one frame, with no error to catch.

This has a name: tearing. It's not a React bug — it's the cost of letting renders be interruptible, and it only shows up once a render can be interrupted.

The hook was never wrong before — it was just never tested like this

Here's the part that catches people: useState + useEffect isn't a bad pattern. It's the correct pattern for state React owns. The problem is specifically external state — state that lives outside React and changes on its own schedule, which is exactly what "subscribe to a browser API" always is.

A useEffect-based subscription updates state after the store already changed, through a callback, on React's own timing. It has no way to ask, right before this component paints, "is this still current?" It just trusts whatever setOnline it last received.

The fix React shipped for exactly this

useSyncExternalStore is the hook React 18 added so you stop hand-rolling this. The shape is unusual the first time you see it — three functions, no state:

import { useSyncExternalStore } from 'react';

function subscribe(callback) {
  window.addEventListener('online', callback);
  window.addEventListener('offline', callback);
  return () => {
    window.removeEventListener('online', callback);
    window.removeEventListener('offline', callback);
  };
}

function getSnapshot() {
  return navigator.onLine;
}

function useOnlineStatus() {
  return useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot);
}

subscribe wires up your listener once, same as the useEffect before. The difference is getSnapshot — a function that reads the current value directly, with nothing cached in React state. React calls it on every render, and critically, it re-checks it synchronously right before committing. If the store moved since the last check, React throws that render away and re-renders immediately with the fresh value, instead of letting a stale one paint. That synchronous re-check is the whole fix: it closes the exact gap where tearing happens.

You're not writing less code than before. You're handing React the one piece of information — "read it fresh, right now" — that a useState callback can never provide after the fact.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

The part that bites on the server

useSyncExternalStore takes an optional third argument, getServerSnapshot, and skipping it is the next trap:

function getServerSnapshot() {
  return true; // sensible default: assume online during SSR
}

useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot);

There's no window on the server, so getSnapshot can't run there — navigator doesn't exist. If your component can render during SSR and you omit getServerSnapshot, React throws rather than guessing. It's not being pedantic: without it, the server-rendered HTML and the first client render would read different realities, and React would rather fail loudly than ship a hydration mismatch silently.

If your component is client-only (inside a dynamic import with SSR disabled, say), you can skip it. If it ever renders on the server, you can't.

You've already used this, you just didn't call it

If you reach for Zustand or react-redux (v8+), you're already running on useSyncExternalStore — it's what those libraries' React bindings switched to for exactly this reason. (Jotai, notably, chose not to — its author has written publicly about trading a small tearing risk for behavior that fits Suspense better.) You don't need to rewrite a working store library. You need this hook for the stores you wrote yourself: the useLocalStorage, useMediaQuery, or useWebSocketMessage hook sitting in your hooks/ folder, quietly subscribing to something outside React with a pattern that was correct until concurrent rendering gave it a seam to fall through.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 6-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

Go find your oldest useState + useEffect-plus-addEventListener hook. If it feeds more than one component, it has a tearing window — you just haven't hit the one render that exposes it yet. What's yours tracking: window size, online status, something else? Tell me in the comments and I'll tell you if it needs the swap.

🚀 Want more like this? Every guide, playground, and quiz lives on bestpractic.org — open it and sign up free so the next one finds you.

Thanks for reading! Let's stay connected:

  • ⭐ GitHub — follow me and star the projects: github.com/parsajiravand
  • 💬 Discord — join the frontend best-practices community: discord.gg/d9KRhuAwQ
  • 📸 Instagram — frontend best practices, daily: @bestpractice___

articles.title: 5 Steps on How to not loose at a hackathon?
articles.description: In 1999, ten developers gathered to work on cryptographic frameworks, IPv6, and IPsec for OpenBSD, in...
articles.body_html:
In 1999, ten developers gathered to work on cryptographic frameworks, IPv6, and IPsec for OpenBSD, in what is often considered the first-ever hackathon. Since then, the tech world has decided that the best way to encourage innovation is to put a few hundred developers in a building, deprive them of sleep, give them unlimited caffeine, and ask them to build something extraordinary in 24 to 48 hours.

Rather surprisingly, it worked.

Hackathons have become places where people build remarkable projects, discover new technologies, make lifelong friends, and occasionally spend six hours debugging something that could have been fixed by restarting their computer.

I started participating in hackathons in my first year of college, eventually began organizing them, and today, as a Hackathon Community Manager at Major League Hacking (@mlhacks), I work with organizers and hackers across the community. Along the way, I've noticed something: some people walk away with incredible experiences but no trophies, while others spend the whole weekend obsessing over winning and miss everything else that makes hackathons worthwhile.

So, how exactly does one avoid losing at a hackathon? Here are five steps. They won't guarantee a prize, although my definition of winning might be slightly different from yours.

Step 1: Talk to People. A Radical Concept, I Know.

You arrive surrounded by hundreds of people who share your interest in building things. Naturally, the sensible move is to find a corner, put on your headphones, and avoid all of them for 36 hours.

Or perhaps not.

Hackathons bring together developers exploring new frameworks, designers who approach problems differently, first-timers discovering what an API is, and veterans who've already made every mistake you're about to make. Talk to them. Ask what they're building and why. You don't need a networking strategy; a simple conversation is usually enough.

Talk to the organizers too. They've spent months on an event you're experiencing over a weekend. And at MLH-supported events, talk to the MLH reps. We're not just there to explain rules and hand out stickers (though stickers are an extremely compelling reason to approach anyone btw). We can connect you with resources, opportunities, and people worth knowing.

You might come looking for a teammate and leave with a mentor, a future collaborator, or someone who shares your inexplicably specific interest in apps for household appliances. You won't find any of them by staring at your terminal.

Step 2: Observe. There's a Lot Happening Beyond Your Screen.

In one corner, someone's building an AI app. Across the room, a team is assembling hardware with a worrying number of exposed wires. Somewhere else, a group has just discovered that the technology they spent twelve hours integrating doesn't support the one feature their project depends on.

Watch how other teams divide work, which tools they try, and how they decide what to do when something breaks. Most importantly, pay attention to how they think. One team might build a complicated ML pipeline while another solves the same problem with simple software and clever design. Neither is automatically better, and understanding why someone chose a solution is often worth more than the solution itself.

(No, this isn't an invitation to copy someone's project or acquire their GitHub repo through questionable means.)

Walk around and attend demos. Hackathons pack enormous amounts of knowledge into small spaces, and it would be a shame to spend the weekend accessing only what's already on your laptop.

Step 3: Ask Questions. Particularly the Ones You Think Are Stupid.

There's a peculiar belief among developers that everyone else knows exactly what they're doing. They don't. Some are just better at maintaining the appearance.

Hackathons give you mentors, workshops, and experienced developers who are all there to help people build things. Use them. If you're stuck, ask. If a workshop covers something unfamiliar, ask. There's no noble reason to spend four hours debugging something someone could explain in ten minutes.

Figuring things out yourself is valuable, and getting thoroughly confused is practically a tradition in software development. But knowing when to ask for help is a skill too. And sometimes the best question isn't "How do I do this?" but "Why did you build it this way?"

Step 4: Build Something Great. Whatever That Means.

Ah, yes. The actual project. You may have noticed we're only getting to it at Step 4. This is intentional.

We've developed strange expectations about what makes a project great. Apparently it must revolutionize education, transform healthcare, end climate change, or use AI to fix an inconvenience humanity has tolerated for centuries. Preferably within 24 hours.

Solving meaningful problems is worthwhile, but not every great hackathon project needs to save the world. Sometimes it solves a small problem exceptionally well, combines existing tools in an interesting way, or, especially for beginners, is simply something you've always wanted to build.

Start with something that interests you. Great ideas often begin with "Wouldn't it be interesting if I could build something that does this?" Maybe that's computer vision, language models on physical hardware, a tool for an annoying task, or just a fun game. When you care about the idea, you'll keep going when something inevitably breaks. And something will inevitably break.

Experiment with technology. Don't just collect it. Hackathons are a great place to try unfamiliar APIs, frameworks, and hardware. But integrating a tool because it improves your project is different from integrating it because its logo looks good on a slide or MLH is giving out a prize for it. Good technical decisions aren't about using the most tools; they're about choosing the right ones.

Step 5: Collect Feedback, Not Just Stickers.

Let me be clear: stickers are important. I've been in the hackathon space for over three years, I work at MLH, and I'm obsessed with a good sticker collection.

But you should also collect feedback.

One of the biggest mistakes is guarding your project like a state secret until judging, only to discover that the feature you spent ten hours perfecting isn't useful to anyone but you. An unfortunate discovery to make three minutes before judging ends.

Share early. Explain your idea to another team, run your approach past a mentor, and show someone a prototype to see if they get it without a fifteen-minute explanation. If they don't, or they suggest something simpler, or they spot a problem you missed, that's all useful information.

And if another team is stuck on something you've solved before, help them. You're not giving away your chances of winning. Hackathons are competitions, but they're also communities, and the two can coexist just fine.

So, Did You Win?

At the end, the judges decide. Some teams win prizes. Most go home without a trophy, presumably after locating their chargers and remembering what uninterrupted sleep feels like.

But consider what you've gained. You met people you wouldn't otherwise have met, explored new technologies, and built something that didn't exist when you arrived. Maybe it worked perfectly. Maybe it worked only during the demo, an achievement deserving its own category of engineering recognition. Or maybe it didn't work at all, but now you know why and what you'd do differently.

Winning a prize is wonderful, so work hard and give the judges every reason to recognize you. Just don't make it the only measure of whether your weekend was worthwhile.

A hackathon is one of those rare competitions where you can lose the judging round and still leave with more than you arrived with.

And if you've managed that, I'd argue you've followed these five steps rather successfully.

MLH Hackathons are the best place to lean, connect and grow in the tech space. So, at your next MLH Hackathon, don't forget to follow the 5 steps and don't forget to grab some awesome stickers and swag!

articles.title: 926 Steps, Two Lobotomies, and Zero Nudges: Flight-Testing the Commitment Machine Across Gemini, Claude, and GPT-OSS
articles.description: A 2026 Harvard study of 718 companies found that AI agents write 30% more code and close zero additional tickets because review times jump 49%. Here is what happened when I put my 1986 Commitment Machine into live production across Gemini, Claude, and GPT-OSS.
articles.body_html:
A 2026 Harvard study of 718 companies found that AI coding agents write 30% more code and close zero extra tickets because PR review times jump 49%. When I ran my 1986 Commitment Machine across five live production tickets, a mid-flight vendor swap, and an open-weight crash test, here is what the flight recorder proved.

"The dashboard with the Mermaid state diagram is perfect. I find myself not even opening the pull requests now. I just wait for the green board or the triage details... And I also like that every code change is paired with an immediate critical reviewer. That one step really reduces friction."

— My notes to myself after the fourth ticket in a row

1. The Bottom Line Up Front: What Live Production Just Proved

Earlier this month, Harvard researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton published a massive study ("Artificial Intelligence in the Firm: Bottlenecks in Software Production", covered in Forkast News) tracking 718 companies and more than 725,000 software developers from 2021 to 2026.

By early 2026, over 95% of those companies had rolled out AI coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Devin). And the numbers they found should make every engineering manager wince:

  • Developers wrote +30% more code (1,500 extra lines per developer per month), and opened +23% more pull requests.
  • Yet the number of finished Jira tickets and epics went up by 0%.
  • Why? Because PR review wait times jumped +49% (+3.45 days), the number of PRs kicked back for rewrites nearly doubled, review comments per PR rose +35%, and 14% more senior engineers got dragged away from their own work to pay what the researchers call the "babysitting tax."

If you've ever worked on a real software team, you don't need an economics degree to spot the bug. If you make typing code 10x faster, but your AI never pushes back on a bad ticket and never catches its own bugs before committing, you haven't sped up your team. You've just aimed a firehose of plausible-looking slop at your senior reviewers.

In Part 3.10, I redesigned my coding workflow (Randal's Public Workflow Gist) specifically to invert that bottleneck—moving ticket pushback, adversarial code review, and state tracking before git commit using Fernando Flores's 1986 "Committed Speech" rules, a 1976 Makefile, and a 1983 /etc/init.d state directory (00_governance.md through 99_next_action.md).

Then I turned the key and ran five consecutive production tickets (926+ steps, 18 subagents), a 960-step mid-flight vendor swap, and a 791-step open-weight torture test through it.

Before we look at the flight logs, here is the bottom line from those runs:

  1. You beat the +30% code-bloat trap before writing a single line of code: When you force a read-only Codebase Archaeologist subagent to check a ticket's claims against git log before the agent is allowed to promise code, stale or already-solved tickets get closed in 8 minutes via a Counter-Offer (0 lines of code written) or trimmed in half—instead of turning into 300-line zombie PRs.
  2. You beat the +49% PR review bottleneck by running an Adversarial Critic before git commit and collapsing bot threads into one table: Pairing every code edit with a local Critic subagent and a single consolidated PR triage comment catches subtle framework bugs (like Flutter's post-await ScaffoldMessenger trap) locally, so the human reviewer doesn't even have to open the GitHub PR page until the board is green.
  3. Keeping state in /etc/init.d files on disk makes your agent both lobotomy-proof and vendor-agnostic: When every commitment lives in numbered Markdown files on disk instead of hidden inside one model's chat RAM, the agent not only survives back-to-back 200k-token context resets without losing its place—you can literally swap Claude Sonnet 4.6 for Gemini 4 at Step 433 of a 960-step run when a quota wall hits, and the new model finishes the job without missing a beat.
  4. External Makefile scaffolding has a hard floor—and a 120B open-weight model fell right through it: A Makefile can keep a capable model (Gemini 4 or Claude Sonnet 4.6) on the rails, but when I put GPT-OSS 120B into the exact same cockpit for 791 steps, it ignored the /etc/init.d files, suffered 6 context lobotomies, searched Google for private local Dart classes, and fork-bombed 6 simultaneous background git commit jobs while deleting .git/index.lock.

2. Why These Five Tickets Matter: Every One of Them Tests a Different Failure Mode

I didn't cherry-pick five easy toy problems. These were simply the next five tickets sitting in our production monorepo backlog—and each one happened to test a specific failure mode where normal AI coding agents create work instead of finishing it:

Ticket & The Failure Mode It Tested Steps / Subagents Context Resets What the Commitment Machine Did Differently Dev Nudges
1. TICKET-553: The Stale / Contradicted Ticket
(Tests whether the agent blindly writes +30% dead code on an obsolete ticket) 		69 steps
1 subagent		 0 Archaeologist proved the requested wrapper was already built and rejected in PR #927 two weeks ago. Issued a Counter-Offer: closed in 8m 29s with 0 lines of code. 0
2. TICKET-779: The Half-Solved Ticket
(Tests whether the agent re-implements work that already landed on main) 		135 steps
3 subagents		 0 Archaeologist proved the .scripts/*.sh pipefail guards had already landed in PR #1029, cutting the scope in half (AGENTS.md 31,248 / 32,000 byte cap only). 0
3. TICKET-482: The Linter Blind Spot & Bot Flood
(Tests whether subtle UI bugs and 14 bot threads get dumped on a human reviewer) 		189 steps
5 subagents		 2 Scoped 19 dialogs down to 15, caught a post-await ScaffoldMessenger bug (SCAR-RIV-14) that flutter analyze missed, and triaged 14 bot comments in 1 table. 0
4. TICKET-891: The Flaky Cloud CI Runner
(Tests whether a transient GitHub Actions hiccup drags a human back to babysit) 		182 steps
4 subagents		 0 Verified all 6 ticket premises in 38s, passed 2 Critic rounds, and automatically re-ran a flaky cloud CI job (gh run rerun --failed) to green. 0
5. TICKET-227: The Double Context Lobotomy
(Tests whether a 351-step math/binary ticket falls apart when the 200k window resets mid-commit) 		351 steps
5 subagents		 2 (233k & 46k) Hit auto-compaction 1 second after I said "ok to commit and push". Woke up, read 00_governance.md..99_next_action.md, and finished 45/45 tests with 0 reminders. 0

Let's walk through how these five tickets, the mid-flight Claude-to-Gemini swap, and the GPT-OSS 120B crash test played out in the transcripts.

3. Finding #1: Beating the +30% Code-Bloat Trap Before Writing a Single Line of Code (TICKET-553, TICKET-779, TICKET-482)

Why did the 718 companies in the Harvard study end up with +30% more code and 0% more finished tickets?

Because in a real engineering backlog, tickets rot. Between the day somebody files a ticket and the day an engineer picks it up, other PRs merge, architecture decisions change, and half the work often gets solved somewhere else.

Hand a normal AI agent a stale ticket, and its "Yes-Man" training (Part 3.9) forces it to say "Certainly!" and write the code anyway:

  • On TICKET-779, the ticket asked to add set -euo pipefail guards to our .scripts/*.sh files and enforce a 32 KB size limit on AGENTS.md. Before writing a plan, my Target 15 Archaeologist checked the repo, proved the .sh scripts already had set -euo pipefail on main, and cut the job in half.
  • On TICKET-482, the ticket listed 19 creation dialogs that needed error-banner handling. The Archaeologist inspected all 19 up front, proved 4 of them were already fixed on main, and scoped the plan strictly to the remaining 15.

And then there was TICKET-553—the poster child for the Harvard study's +30% code bloat.

TICKET-553 was a High priority ticket asking the developer to build a pre-signout wrapper (PreSignOutFirebaseAuth) that deletes the user's push-notification token from the database before calling FirebaseAuth.instance.signOut().

If you only look at today's files on HEAD, that wrapper isn't there—so a standard AI agent would happily crank out ~280 lines of code across 4 files and open a pull request.

Instead, my Target 15 Codebase Archaeologist ran git log -p across recent history (SCAR-ARCH-20) and wrote down a devastating finding in 15_archaeology_receipt.md:

  • Two weeks after TICKET-553 was filed, a developer working on a sibling ticket in PR #927 had already written that exact 243-line PreSignOutFirebaseAuth wrapper!
  • During code review on PR #927, our human lead architect explicitly rejected the wrapper, explaining that wrapping FirebaseAuth is brittle across SDK upgrades and unnecessary because post-signout cleanup + server-side pruning already handles stale tokens. A follow-up commit deleted the wrapper before PR #927 merged—leaving the older duplicate TICKET-553 sitting forgotten in the backlog like an unexploded bomb!

Because our workflow stamps any ticket claim that collides with codebase history as CONTRADICTED, the agent was forbidden to promise code. Instead, it came back to me with a Counter-Offer:

  • Plan A (Recommended — 0 files, 0 lines of code): Accept the Archaeologist's receipt, skip coding, post the PR #927 history onto TICKET-553, and close the ticket.
  • Plan B (4 files, ~280 lines of code): Overrule the lead architect and build the rejected wrapper anyway.

My entire review took four seconds: "plan A is fine. If he has already spoken, I'm not challenging."

Even better, because our workflow is a 1976 Makefile rather than a rigid 21-step checklist, an approved plan with zero target files didn't require any GOTO spaghetti: Target 30 (code), Target 40 (critic), Target 50 (commit), Target 60 (push), and Target 70 (PR checks) all reported Up to date (Nothing to be done) automatically, jumping straight to Target 80 to document and close the issue in 8 minutes, 29 seconds.

4. Finding #2: Beating the +49% Review Bottleneck with Pre-Commit Critics and One-Shot Bot Triage (TICKET-482)

What happens when a ticket does require changing 15 files across four packages?

In the Harvard study, developers push the AI's first green test straight to GitHub, where human reviewers wait 3.45 days only to bounce the PR back (2x bounce rate) or drown in +35% more bot comments.

In TICKET-482 (PR #1234), we saw how the Commitment Machine stops both problems before a human ever opens the PR:

A. Catching a Sneaky Flutter Linter Blind Spot (SCAR-RIV-14)

While updating the 15 creation dialogs so failed saves keep the modal open and display an error banner, the agent wrote the textbook Flutter pattern to satisfy the use_build_context_synchronously lint—capturing ScaffoldMessenger.of(context) and AppLocalizations.of(context) before the await line:

// Captured before the await so use_build_context_synchronously is happy:
final messenger = ScaffoldMessenger.of(context);
final local = AppLocalizations.of(context);

final result = await notifier.create(...);
isLoading.value = false;

// ⚠️ THE LINTER BLIND SPOT (SCAR-RIV-14):
notifier.onCreated(result, messenger, local);
if (!result.hasError && result.hasValue && context.mounted) {
  Navigator.of(context).pop(result.value);
}

Because the word context doesn't appear inside notifier.onCreated(result, messenger, local), flutter analyze --fatal-infos passed with 0 warnings!

Yet if the user closes the modal while await notifier.create(...) is waiting on the network, messenger (which belongs to the parent screen behind the dialog) is still alive—so notifier.onCreated(...) pops up a ghost SnackBar on the parent screen after the modal is already gone!

Instead of a senior engineer having to catch that subtle bug on GitHub three days later:

  1. Our automated review triage (Target 70) flagged the unguarded post-await call.
  2. The TDD Implementation Engineer wrote a Completer<void> widget test that closed the dialog mid-flight and proved the ghost SnackBar bug failed (red_exit = 1).
  3. It wrapped notifier.onCreated, any post-await ref.read(...), and Navigator.pop inside a single outer if (context.mounted) { ... } block (green_exit = 0), and a fresh Round 2 Model: "pro" Adversarial Critic (40_critic_review.md) verified all 14 dialogs before asking me to land.
  4. At Target 90, that trap was permanently recorded as SCAR-RIV-14 so no future agent gets fooled by pre-await ScaffoldMessenger handles.

B. One-Comment Bot Triage & The Mermaid Cockpit (SCAR-PROC-127)

When the GitHub review bot flagged that context.mounted pattern across 14 dialog files (C-1..C-14), our old rules would have burned 28 separate API calls (14 REST +1 reactions + 14 GraphQL resolveReviewThread calls) just closing threads one by one.

At Step 330, I made a simple observation: "generally, we just post one final PR comment instead of closing threads... Yeah, per-thread resolution burns a lot of redundant tokens." That became SCAR-PROC-127: the agent posts one consolidated PR triage table (gh pr comment <PR> --body-file <scratch>/triage_comment.md), paired with our 2-Push Bot Circuit Breaker (SCAR-REVIEW-27) so the agent never gets stuck in an endless ping-pong loop over minor Round 2 bot nitpicks.

And because 99_next_action.md renders a live color-coded Mermaid Commitment Diagram (:::done green, :::active blue, :::gate gold) right in my IDE sidebar, I don't even open the GitHub PR page anymore—I just wait for the green board.

5. Finding #3: /etc/init.d Files Make Your Agent Both Lobotomy-Proof (TICKET-227) and Vendor-Agnostic (Claude -> Gemini at Step 433)

The third reason long AI coding sessions fail in production is that the model either runs out of context tokens (200k lobotomy) or runs out of provider quota halfway through a big ticket.

Because our workflow keeps all commitment state in numbered Unix files on disk (<brain>/state/00_governance.md through 99_next_action.md) and forces subagents (fork()) to do the heavy reading and testing in their own throwaway windows (SCAR-PROC-95), we survived two extreme stress tests:

  1. Surviving Two Context Resets (TICKET-227): On TICKET-227 (351 steps, 45 unit tests), the IDE hit its context limit and triggered auto-compaction (CHECKPOINT) at Step 188 (233,658 -> 43,077 tokens)—literally 1 second after I typed "ok to commit and push"—and then hit a second reset at Step 350. In a normal chat session, getting lobotomized right after "ok to commit and push" is fatal: the model forgets whether the Critic ran or what it was about to commit. With Target 00: read-init-d, the agent woke up on Step 189, read 00_governance.md through 99_next_action.md off the disk, and picked up on the very next tool call with 0 nudges.
  2. Swapping Claude Sonnet 4.6 for Gemini 4 in Mid-Air (Step 433 of 960): During a marathon 960-step UI verification run on PR #1234 (FT-184, booting local emulators and driving an iOS Simulator to capture 5 live screenshots), Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Thinking) hit its provider quota wall and died at Step 432. Instead of starting over, I clicked the IDE model picker, switched from Claude Sonnet 4.6 to Gemini 4, and typed "continue". At Step 434, Gemini 4 read the /etc/init.d files Claude had written to disk, saw the exact target state, fixed the Xcode 26 simulator window issue in 20 steps, captured all 5 iOS screenshots, and finished the run!

When your workflow state lives in plain text files on disk instead of inside one vendor's context window, the LLM is just a swappable CPU running against a persistent hard drive.

6. Finding #4: The Capability Floor—Why GPT-OSS 120B Crashed and Burned in the Same Cockpit (791 Steps)

That mid-flight swap from Claude to Gemini begged the obvious question:

If the smarts live in the external Makefile and /etc/init.d files on disk, how small or cheap a model can wear the suit? Can you drop an open-weight 120B model into the exact same cockpit and get a senior engineer for free?

To find out, I took TICKET-894 ("Harden entity fromJson deserialization for legacy creator keys, timestamps, and nested maps"—the follow-up ticket split out of TICKET-482) and ran an A/B test in the exact same IDE with the exact same rules and tools: first with open-weight GPT-OSS 120B (Medium) for 791 steps (67 minutes) until I pulled the plug, and then with Gemini 4 (FT-222), which finished the ticket cleanly with 0 nudges.

Here is the scorecard from that 791-step crash test:

What Happened on TICKET-894 Frontier Model (Gemini 4) Open-Weight Test (GPT-OSS 120B) Why GPT-OSS 120B Failed
/etc/init.d State Files (<brain>/state/*.md) 100% (00..99 written) 0 files created Ignored SKILL.md and Turn-1 rules completely.
fork() Subagents Spawned (SCAR-PROC-95) 100% (Archaeologist, TDD, Critic) 0 subagents forked Dumped all 104 shell commands and 52 file reads into the main window.
Context Lobotomies (CHECKPOINT) 0 6 compactions (Steps 119..772) Flooded its own window, then woke up with total amnesia 6 times.
Botched Tool Calls (ERROR_MESSAGE) 0 (0.0%) 50 errors (13.6% of turns) Printed raw JSON tool syntax inside its <thinking> block with empty output.
Searching Google for Private Local Code 0 13 calls (search_web) Used Google Web Search to look for private Dart classes inside our own repo!
Simultaneous Background git commit Jobs 1 (waited cleanly) 6 running at once Set WaitMsBeforeAsync: 0 on git commit, then ran rm -f .git/index.lock while commits were still alive!
Outcome Merged (0 nudges) Aborted at Step 791 (18 nudges) Failed to finish any of the 4 ticket items.

Two scenes from GPT-OSS 120B's flight recorder tell the whole story:

  • Finding ParseLegacy, Getting Lobotomized, and Searching Google for It (Steps 90–213): At Step 91 (after I nudged it to stop searching Google and run rg locally), GPT-OSS 120B found ParseLegacy in packages/helpers/lib/src/json/json.dart and noted in its thoughts that ParseLegacy already handled int and map. Because it never wrote 15_archaeology_receipt.md to disk, Compaction #1 hit at Step 119 and wiped that file path from its memory. Waking up with no /etc/init.d files on disk, GPT-OSS 120B called Google Web Search (search_web(query: "ParseLegacy")) twice (Steps 192 & 196), announced "I'm still not seeing the ParseLegacy implementation in this repository", and spent the next 580 steps inventing a brand-new duplicate ParseLegacyAuth class from scratch!
  • Zero-Millisecond git commit Fork-Bombing (Steps 480–710): On 7 of its 10 git commit calls, GPT-OSS 120B passed WaitMsBeforeAsync: 0—backgrounding git commit #1 after 0 milliseconds while it still held .git/index.lock. On the next turn, it fired git commit #2, hit Unable to create '.git/index.lock': File exists, ran rm -f .git/index.lock while git commit #1 was still running, and launched five more background git commit jobs all corrupting the same Git index at once!

The Four "Driver's License" Checks for Any Autonomous Model

Why can Gemini 4 (Low) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 cruise through the Makefile workflow with zero repeat regressions, while GPT-OSS 120B drove straight into a ditch?

Because an external checklist and dashboard can replace deep puzzle-solving (Low vs. High thinking), but they cannot help a driver who can't read the steering wheel. Before any model can use a Makefile and /etc/init.d harness, it must pass four basic "driver's license" checks:

  1. Turn-1 Rule Obedience: Does it actually open SKILL.md and create 00_governance.md on Turn 1 before editing code?
  2. Clean Tool Calling: Can it invoke tools cleanly without dumping raw JSON inside its <thinking> thoughts?
  3. Basic Tool Sense: Does it know to search local files with rg instead of Google Web Search, and to wait for git commit instead of backgrounding it after 0ms?
  4. Honest Error Reporting: When a tool returns ERROR, does it report the failure honestly instead of hallucinating "I've posted the plan to Linear!"?

7. Summary: What the Commitment Machine Delivers—And What Comes Next

When you put the Harvard study's 718-company bottleneck next to these 2,677 steps of live production telemetry (926 steps across 5 tickets + 960 steps on FT-184 + 791 steps on GPT-OSS 120B), the takeaway is crystal clear:

  • Don't optimize for typing speed (+30% LOC); optimize for pre-commit truth (Counter-Offers + Local Critics). Making it legal—and mandatory—for an Archaeologist subagent to stamp a bad ticket CONTRADICTED (TICKET-553) and for a local Adversarial Critic to catch subtle framework bugs (TICKET-482) before git commit is how you keep junk out of your human reviewers' queues.
  • Put your agent's brain on the filesystem (/etc/init.d), not in the context window. Plain numbered Markdown files on disk turn 200k-token context resets and mid-flight vendor quota walls (Claude Sonnet 4.6 -> Gemini 4 at Step 433) into minor speed bumps.
  • Respect the model capability floor. Give the Makefile suit to a frontier model (Gemini 4 or Claude Sonnet 4.6) that passes the four Driver's License checks—and save the sub-threshold local models for Part 9, where we'll train those exact four reflexes directly into the weights via LoRA / DPO.

Next Up in Part 3.12: "Is This a Step, or Is This a Sensor?"

Right after I published Part 3.10, systems programmers, security researchers, compiler writers, and even an autonomous AI agent running on Claude Opus 5.5 started red-teaming the Commitment Machine in the comments—asking:

  • "The Makefile stops a check from being skipped—but what stops the agent from faking the green light when it controls the test file too?" (Sam LABBE & howcani howcani)
  • "Once RETRACTED is a legal move, what stops a lazy agent from claiming a method doesn't exist just to bail out of a hard ticket?" (Dawn / Sentient_Dawn)
  • "Why do prompt files rewritten by LLMs bloat by +145.8% and turn sharp numbers into mush—and how do you scale past 500 Scars without blowing up your context window?" (Vinnie Falco, Ctbhatia, & Subhadeep Chatterjee)

In Part 3.12, we'll look at how their feedback upgraded our workflow with read-only test pins, Linux insmod Loadable Scar Modules, and package:synthetic_scars_lint—turning prompt scars into 15ms compiler auto-fixes that cost zero prompt tokens and zero LLM retry turns.

articles.title: PHP vulnerability PHP2Shell: what the October 21 emergency release fixed and what is still disputed
articles.description: PHP2Shell is two critical PHP remote code execution flaws fixed on October 21, 2026. A plain-language look at the bugs, the leaked embargo, who reports exploitation, and
articles.body_html:
The PHP vulnerability called PHP2Shell is two critical flaws in the PHP engine itself, fixed in an emergency release on October 21, 2026. PHP runs an estimated 70% of websites according to the Guardian and Wiz, so the question for a developer is simple: which copies of PHP do you run, and are they patched? The better story is how the bug waited two years for a decision, how the embargo leaked, and why sources disagree about exploitation.

TL;DR

  • PHP2Shell covers CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both rated 9.2 on CVSS v4.0 by the PHP team. Fixed releases are PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. PHP 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 got source patches only.
  • The flaws sit in memory and error handling, which nearly every request touches. On Apache with mod_php the first one can run before any application code, so a login page cannot stop it.
  • A PHP core developer saw the first signs in a 2024 audit. Competing fixes had trade-offs and a consensus-based security team struggled to choose. The PHP Foundation calls the delay a structural failure.
  • Amazon logged an attempt on October 17, four days before the patch. CISA had not observed exploitation at publication, and several analysts say many public exploit scripts do not work. Patch anyway.
  • The same day GitLab shipped a critical patch release, and a New Mexico court ordered Meta to pay $25 billion.

What is the PHP vulnerability called PHP2Shell?

PHP2Shell is the nickname for two flaws that let an unauthenticated stranger run code on a server through ordinary web requests. The official advisories are GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w for CVE-2026-109618, titled "RCE via OOM corruption", and GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp for CVE-2026-109619, titled "RCE via stale global state". The earliest affected code path dates to PHP 5.4.0.

PHP is a scripting language that builds web pages on the server just before they reach the visitor. It is over thirty years old, and WordPress, Drupal and MediaWiki are written in it. The Guardian describes the nonprofit PHP Foundation as having about thirteen full-time and part-time engineers, which matters for the rest of the story.

Wiz points out that the problem sits in PHP itself, below whatever application runs on top. Even a hello world script on an affected version is exposed, so the WordPress, Drupal and Joomla demonstrations are examples.

How does PHP remote code execution work here, in plain words?

No exploit steps appear here. The mechanism is explained at the level the PHP advisories use.

The first flaw starts with memory limits. Every PHP request gets a memory budget. If a request hits that limit at exactly the wrong moment, PHP exits the current work in a hurry and can leave the request memory half built. The cleanup step may later read or branch on that half-built data. On Apache with mod_php the cleanup runs even when request startup failed, entirely before application code begins. PHP-FPM removes the child when startup fails, which blocks that path, although the advisory says FPM is still susceptible through other routes.

The second flaw is a leftover. A worker keeps some global state between requests, such as error, session and object state. A fatal error can abandon an operation before it resets that state, so the worker holds a pointer to memory that belonged to the previous request. A later request handled by the same worker can then use that stale pointer before normal initialization replaces it.

The fix removes PHP's emergency exit for running out of memory. Instead of bailing out of the middle of a request, PHP now schedules a graceful stop at the next safe point, and it only hard-stops past a second, higher threshold. Both advisories say updating to a patched release is the only complete mitigation. Partial measures exist, and PHP's team says they only reduce exposure.

Why did a known PHP memory bug wait two years?

The PHP Foundation's post-mortem is unusually frank. In 2024 PHP had its first external security audit in years, funded by the Sovereign Tech Agency and carried out by Quarkslab. While fixing one reported issue, a Foundation-contracted core developer found the first signs of the out-of-memory problem. A potential exploit was theorized, but no concrete vector was found and other issues with clear impact took priority.

Fixing it was hard. Each competing approach had a cost: broken backward compatibility, new denial-of-service risk, or changes to many third-party extensions. The team decides by consensus and, in the Foundation's words, "struggled to choose between these and feared the repercussions of shipping the wrong choice." Work stalled and restarted for months. The Foundation says plainly that the delay was a structural failure caused by the decision process and a lack of resources, and that the team is moving to majority decisions and bringing leadership in sooner on hard trade-offs.

Who found PHP2Shell, and did AI find it?

In August, finders arrived within days. Calif began a PHP audit on July 30 under OpenAI's Patch the Planet program, and researcher Ryan Austin reported the first bug on August 11. OpenAI independently reported the same root cause the same day, and Wiz, using Wiz Atlas, Google's Gemini 4 Argon and OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, found and reported variants on August 24.

How much the models mattered is contested. OpenAI said frontier AI was key. Calif's own write-up says no special harness or non-public model was used in the initial discovery, and credits a theory about where PHP's old bugs hide. Chainguard's CEO told The Register his team independently found the same bugs on a Friday night with a basic prompt asking for bad vulnerabilities in PHP. The common thread is that finding this class of bug got much cheaper, and a months-long embargo now has to survive that.

How did the PHP2Shell embargo leak?

The coordinated release was set for October 22 at 14:00 UTC. According to the Foundation, on Tuesday October 20 around 15:00 UTC the two CVE IDs began circulating on forums and social media with a wrong release time and a wrong score of 10.0. The Hacker News post that carried them reached 282 points. PHP published a pre-announcement at 19:30 UTC and moved the release forward a day.

Around 20:00 UTC Calif mistakenly published a video of its proof of concept, and copies circulated after it was deleted. On Wednesday at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the release, Chainguard published built images containing the fix. The Foundation says any attacker could study the fix in binary form while everyone else waited. A patch is also a diff, and attackers read diffs.

Chainguard's CEO says the company did not leak, that people were already being hit, and that it made the call to ship the fixes. The timeline itself is not in dispute.

Is PHP2Shell being exploited? What the sources say

  • Amazon Threat Intelligence logged an exploitation attempt on a honeypot on October 17 and more attempts on October 21 from different infrastructure. It says it is unclear whether those attempts would have worked on real systems, and later said PHP2Shell is broadly exploited.
  • watchTowr reported exploitation in the wild through its honeypot network. Cloudflare's CEO said it saw thousands of attempts in the ten hours before the announcement and millions by Thursday morning.
  • CISA said it had not observed exploitation as of publication. The PHP team said it identified no functional exploit at release.
  • watchTowr also says many exploit scripts flying around crash or do nothing. VulnCheck, as relayed by Tanium, found code execution works in some setups and that none of the public ones beat memory randomization on standard x86-64. Researcher Elias Taylor argues the bug is nowhere near as easy as Log4Shell, and still says patch.

An attempt is only a knock on the door. Amazon's advice is to investigate from at least October 17.

Which PHP versions get a PHP security update?

Fixed releases are 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. For 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 the PHP project published minimal source patches only. Older versions get nothing from the PHP project, and distributions may backport fixes, so ask your vendor. PHP 8.2 itself reaches end of life on December 31, 2026.

Governments did not wait. The NSA told organizations that could not patch to take PHP systems offline, and the UK's National Cyber Security Centre gave similar advice. The Guardian reports that Dutch sites including the national digital identity service, a Paris police site and several UK council sites went offline, and that Wikimedia took systems down as a precaution. Palo Alto Networks counted more than 22 million exposed instances.

What to do about PHP2Shell tonight

CISA's guidance is a good checklist: inventory every system that runs PHP, including copies inside other software, patch internet-facing systems first, and take PHP systems offline if you cannot update. Restart the workers after updating. Review logs back to October 17 for memory-limit errors and PHP workers launching shells.

This is the same lesson as the previous Daily Diff episode on eMudhra: a fix existing is not the same as the running process having it.

Two other stories from the same day

GitLab shipped critical patch releases, led by 19.5.1, on October 21. Its advisory describes an integer overflow in the regular expression compiler that could let an unauthenticated user execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server. It is CVE-2026-110264 with a CVSS 3.1 score of 10.0, affecting versions back to 7.0. GitLab.com is already patched; self-managed installations need the update.

In New Mexico, a judge ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in penalties in the state's Cambridge Analytica case, according to CNBC. The jury counted more than 43 million violations at up to $5,000 each, and the filing shows $219.5 billion awarded before it was reduced to $25 billion. Meta's chief legal officer said the company is confident it will prevail on appeal. It is a court order that Meta is appealing.

Verdict: SHIP IT

I would ship the PHP update tonight. The new version number is the only complete fix, the exploitation picture is disputed but real attempts exist, and the cost of an unneeded restart is small compared with a compromised server.

FAQ

Is PHP2Shell a zero-day?
Amazon logged an attempt four days before the fix, but the sources do not establish that any attempt succeeded. Call it a critical flaw with disputed exploitation.

Do WAF rules or config changes replace patching?
No. PHP, Amazon and the other vendors say updating is the only complete fix. Edge rules and settings such as limiting upload size reduce some paths.

What if I run an unsupported PHP version?
Ask your distribution for a backport, apply PHP's source patches for 7.4, 8.0 or 8.1 if you build from source, or plan a move to a supported version.

articles.title: I Turned a $50 Pocket Computer Into an Occult Operating System Because Modern Computing Has Lost Its Mind
articles.description: 16 applications. A Daedric interface. Generative synthesis, wireless reconnaissance, experimental...
articles.body_html:
16 applications. A Daedric interface. Generative synthesis, wireless reconnaissance, experimental motion sensing, and a tiny browser for the forgotten internet. All running on an ESP32-S3.

There's something profoundly irritating about how boring computers have become.

We have absurd amounts of processing power. Graphics hardware capable of simulating realistic lighting. Neural networks that can generate entire applications while confidently inventing three nonexistent dependencies. Yet practically every interface looks like it escaped from the same corporate design meeting.

Rounded rectangles. Carefully selected shades of gray. A sidebar. Another sidebar. A button that used to do something useful but now opens a subscription page.

Your computer has sixteen cores and apparently the imagination of an insurance company.

Meanwhile, a tiny ESP32-S3 with a 240 × 135 display is perfectly capable of becoming a synthesizer, a network observatory, a procedural graphics machine, and a portal to the weirder corners of the internet.

So I built something called DIVINER.

It's a custom firmware environment for the M5Stack Cardputer ADV, containing sixteen applications inside a hand-crafted Daedric interface. Wireless networks become constellations. Bluetooth devices drift across the display like strange little familiars. Mathematical expressions produce audio. The menu is written in the fictional alphabet from Morrowind, and its glyphs dissolve into English when you navigate through it.

Some of the software is genuinely practical. Some of it is experimental. Some of it exists because I believe a computer should occasionally do something that makes you wonder whether it's entirely pleased to see you.

The complete source code is available here:

DIVINER on GitHub

And the hardware project, build details, and development documentation live here:

DIVINER on Hackaday.io

The firmware is open source. There's a prebuilt binary in the repository, and a desktop simulator for anyone interested in exploring the software without owning the hardware.

But the part worth discussing isn't simply that I managed to cram sixteen applications into a small computer.

It's why I wanted to.

We Used to Let Computers Be Weird

There was a period when interacting with a computer felt like entering somebody else's peculiar universe.

Amiga workbenches. Macintosh System 7. Shareware applications with interfaces designed by people who had clearly never been introduced to a branding consultant. Late-night BBS systems. Software with obscure keyboard shortcuts, ugly but memorable icons, and documentation written like the author had personally declared war on conventional typography.

Not all of it was good.

A fair amount was objectively terrible.

But at least it was identifiable.

You could recognize an application by its personality. Interfaces weren't all desperately trying to disappear. Some of them practically demanded that you learn their internal logic.

I miss that.

I don't particularly want my computer to feel invisible. I want it to feel like an instrument.

DIVINER came out of that frustration, mixed with an unreasonable affection for Morrowind, Serial Experiments Lain, experimental music software, and tiny machines that look like they were designed to receive messages from abandoned satellites.

The idea was simple enough: stop treating the Cardputer as a miniature smartphone and start treating it as a completely different kind of computer.

Not a dashboard. Not a gadget full of unrelated demonstrations.

An environment.

The Hardware Is Ridiculously Small. That's the Point.

The M5Stack Cardputer ADV is built around an ESP32-S3.

It has a compact keyboard, a small color display, wireless connectivity, audio hardware, and enough interfaces to become surprisingly useful without attaching an entire graveyard of external peripherals.

Its screen contains exactly 32,400 pixels.

For perspective, that's not much real estate when you're trying to build a custom interface, display network information, render procedural graphics, and interact with multiple independent applications.

You cannot simply shrink a modern desktop interface down and expect things to work.

Every unnecessary panel becomes expensive. Every poorly designed menu becomes an obstruction. Every line of text needs to justify the pixels it occupies.

And that's when things get interesting.

Constraints force decisions.

A high-resolution monitor can conceal mediocre interface design under layers of padding and decorative nonsense. A 240 × 135 screen gives you nowhere to hide.

DIVINER uses the limitations deliberately.

The primary interface is dark, spare, and aggressive. A blood-and-ember palette. Sharp typography. Subtle audiovisual feedback. Animations that serve the interaction rather than existing to impress a design portfolio.

At least, that's the practical explanation.

The less respectable explanation is that I wanted the thing to look like a cursed piece of consumer electronics from 2001.

Sixteen Applications, or Sixteen Rites

DIVINER doesn't refer to its applications as apps.

It calls them rites.

Yes, that's theatrical. No, I don't particularly care.

They're organized into four domains: Sound, Sight, The Wired, and Wards.

The naming gives the environment a vocabulary of its own, but underneath it is fairly straightforward modular C++ software.

And the applications are not just variations of the same scanning utility.

Sound: Turning an ESP32 Into an Instrument

The first domain contains three separate sound engines.

DRONE is a five-voice generative synthesizer. It combines drifting voices, resonant low-pass filtering, wind-like textures, bell elements, and delay.

It's designed less for writing conventional melodies and more for generating evolving sound environments.

Think unstable ambient textures rather than cheerful ringtone synthesis.

SEQ is a miniature groovebox with kick, snare, hi-hat, acid-style synthesis, Euclidean fills, four pattern banks, song mode, and save/load functionality.

This is where the firmware starts becoming an actual portable musical instrument instead of a curiosity.

BEAT is a bytebeat livecoding environment.

If you're unfamiliar with bytebeat, the premise is beautifully deranged: mathematical expressions involving a time variable can generate audio samples directly.

A tiny expression can produce rhythmic structures, melodies, grinding digital noise, or something resembling a malfunctioning modem experiencing a personal crisis.

All without conventional audio samples.

DIVINER's audio path operates at 24 kHz on the device, with shared DSP utilities supporting its sound-generating applications.

One of the things I enjoy about this arrangement is that the machine doesn't require a computer to explain itself. You can type into the little keyboard and produce sound directly.

No DAW startup sequence. No plugin manager. No seventeen-minute tutorial on configuring an audio interface.

Just an expression and whatever strange noise emerges from it.

Sight: Mathematical Hallucinations

The second domain deals with procedural visuals.

WIRED renders ASCII-based 3D objects, including toruses, wireframe geometry, tunnels, and a navigation sphere.


VISIONS produces animated plasma fields, falling Daedric glyphs, an Oblivion-inspired gate, ash-fire effects, and a heptagram kaleidoscope.

ORACLE casts three runes accompanied by bell-like audio.


No, the rune generator will not predict your future.

Although if it starts correctly predicting compiler errors, I'll reconsider that position.

The graphics applications are interesting because so much visual character can emerge from relatively simple mathematical operations.

You don't need a sophisticated graphics pipeline to make something feel alive.

You need movement, timing, recognizable patterns, and a little willingness to be strange.

I've always liked the idea that procedural graphics are a form of visual synthesis. You're not displaying a completed image. You're describing the rules by which an image continuously comes into existence.

On a tiny display, that distinction matters.

The Invisible World Is More Interesting Than Your Home Screen

The third domain is where DIVINER turns toward networking.

And this is probably the part that will interest the hardware hackers and security researchers.

We spend our lives surrounded by wireless infrastructure. Access points, Bluetooth peripherals, local devices, broadcasts, background activity.

An enormous amount of communication is happening in the air around us, and most people experience absolutely none of it.

Their phone displays a Wi-Fi icon.

That's the entire interface to the invisible machinery surrounding them.

I find that weird.

DIVINER experiments with making that information visible, audible, and spatial.

SCRY transforms nearby Wi-Fi networks into a constellation.

KIN represents discovered Bluetooth devices as drifting familiars.

LISTEN provides receive-only channel monitoring with an audible representation of activity.

LINK handles conventional Wi-Fi connectivity, remembered networks, and captive-portal detection.

NET explores hosts, names, and exposed ports on a local network.

These tools don't all have the same purpose.

Some are diagnostic. Some are informational. Some are experiments in presenting familiar data through an unfamiliar interface.

The central question is whether a network scanner has to look like a network scanner.

Why should access points always appear as a depressing list of SSIDs?

Why couldn't their relationships become part of the interface?

An alternative visualization doesn't automatically make information more accurate or actionable. It can introduce new ambiguities, and that's worth acknowledging.

But the conventional presentation isn't sacred either.

Sometimes changing how information is displayed changes which questions you're inclined to ask.

And occasionally it just looks significantly cooler.

Both are acceptable motivations for making software.

Yes, It Has Experimental Wi-Fi Motion Sensing

The fourth domain, Wards, contains some of the more ambitious and technically uncertain work.

PULSE explores Wi-Fi Channel State Information, or CSI, for detecting changes associated with movement and presence.


The interesting concept here is that wireless communication isn't occurring in a perfectly static environment.

Signals reflect, scatter, and interact with physical surroundings.

When those surroundings change, properties of the observed radio channel can change too.

Under suitable conditions, CSI measurements can provide information related to motion.

This doesn't mean the Cardputer has suddenly acquired magical radar abilities.

Radio-based presence sensing is complicated. Multipath effects, hardware behavior, environmental noise, available traffic, and physical layout all influence what can actually be inferred.

An observed change does not necessarily mean a human walked past the device.

That uncertainty is precisely what makes it worth experimenting with.

I think there's something fascinating about repurposing a communications radio as a crude environmental sensor. It's the same physical hardware, but you're asking it a completely different question.

SENTINEL takes another approach to environmental monitoring.


It learns a baseline of nearby devices, then flags newly observed ones. It also looks for wireless indicators potentially associated with drones.

That last part needs a qualification: it's heuristic. A radio signature is not definitive proof that an object is a drone, and the absence of such a signature doesn't prove there isn't one.

Still, baselining a local wireless environment and watching for changes is an interesting foundation for experimentation.

PROBE adds active HTTP reconnaissance and default-credential checks for explicitly authorized hosts.

The firmware's security-oriented capabilities are intended for equipment and networks the operator owns or has permission to test. It doesn't implement phishing or denial-of-service functions.

The goal is observation and assessment, not turning a handheld computer into an indiscriminate nuisance machine.

We have enough of those already. Most of them are employed in marketing.

There's a Gemini Browser in Here Because Apparently I Have Priorities

This is one of my favorite details.

DIVINER includes GEMINI, a gemtext browser using TLS, with posting support.

Gemini, for anyone unfamiliar, is a lightweight document-oriented internet protocol with a much simpler model than the modern web.

It's closer in spirit to the idea that you should be able to retrieve and read a document without loading half a megabyte of JavaScript, asking permission to accept cookies, and being offered a discount on a newsletter you never wanted.

The Cardputer is an oddly appropriate place to browse it.

A small keyboard. A tiny display. Modest hardware resources.

Nothing about the device suggests that it should be pretending to run a full contemporary browser.

But Gemini doesn't demand that.

There's a satisfying symmetry to using a deliberately minimal computer to access a deliberately minimal part of the internet.

Modern web development has become an extraordinary exercise in industrial-scale complexity.

Sometimes I just want a page containing words.

Preferably without a chatbot asking if I need help finding the words.

The Most Useful Part Might Actually Be the Desktop Simulator

Here's the less glamorous engineering detail that deserves more attention.

DIVINER isn't built exclusively for the physical Cardputer.

It also has a native SDL2 simulator.

This is significant because developing embedded graphical software can be extraordinarily annoying.

Change a few pixels. Recompile. Flash the firmware. Restart. Navigate through the menu. Check whether the animation looks right. Discover that the animation still looks wrong.

Repeat until the sun goes out.

Instead, DIVINER separates application behavior from the hardware through dedicated abstraction layers.

The device implementation handles the actual Cardputer display, keyboard, and audio system.

The native implementation runs the interface on a desktop computer, reproducing the 240 × 135 display at an enlarged scale.

It also supports audio output, WAV recording, scripted input, and headless screenshot generation.

The native network implementation uses simulated data, so it isn't pretending to reproduce actual radio conditions. Wireless functionality still needs to be validated on the physical device.

But graphical and audio development can happen without constantly involving the hardware.

That's a meaningful architectural improvement.

It makes experimentation cheaper in time, which is often the most expensive resource in a project like this.

It also makes the firmware easier for other developers to investigate.

They don't necessarily need to own a Cardputer just to examine the interface or experiment with some of the application code.

For me, this is an important part of what open-source embedded software should be doing.

Not merely releasing code, but making the code practical to explore.

Building and Installing DIVINER

The firmware is written in C++ and built with PlatformIO.

The repository includes source code, build configuration, screenshots, interface previews, a desktop simulator, and a prebuilt firmware image.

To compile for the Cardputer ADV:

pio run -e cardputer

The generated firmware is located at:

.pio/build/cardputer/firmware.bin

To build the desktop simulator:

pio run -e native

And to launch it:

.pio/build/native/program

The firmware is designed to work with the Cardputer Launcher, allowing installation from an SD card or supported USB serial workflow.

Replacing the factory firmware can erase the existing device installation, so back up the device first and follow the current instructions in the repository.

One other important detail: this project specifically targets the Cardputer ADV. Don't assume hardware compatibility with earlier Cardputer models simply because their names are similar.

The full installation process and current files are available in the repository:

github.com/numbpill3d/cardputer-adv-diviner

Why the Interface Is Written in Daedric

I could claim that the Daedric interface is some elaborate experiment in cognitive ergonomics.

And, well, parts of it are genuinely interesting from an interaction-design standpoint.

But the actual reason is simpler.

I like fictional alphabets, strange old software, and the idea that a computer might possess a little mythology of its own.

The main menu displays application names in a hand-rasterized Daedric script. When you navigate to an entry, the characters dissolve into ordinary English.

It's a little theatrical.

It also communicates selection state without requiring additional interface furniture.

There's a lesson in that somewhere.

Decorative systems don't necessarily have to remain decorative. An animation can become a navigational cue. A fictional alphabet can establish atmosphere while also organizing interaction. Sound design can communicate state changes without consuming screen space.

Obviously, none of this would be particularly useful if the machine became impossible to navigate.

An interface that values personality still has to function.

But I reject the premise that usability requires everything to look like the settings screen on a corporate tablet.

There are other ways to make software understandable.

And I'd rather explore them than spend the rest of my life selecting between twelve slightly different border radii.

The Trouble With Calling Everything a Tool

Something else bothers me about the modern maker ecosystem.

We tend to evaluate small computers almost exclusively by the number of recognizable tasks they can perform.

Can it scan Wi-Fi?

Can it send infrared commands?

Can it identify devices?

Can it run this or that utility?

Those are useful questions, but they're incomplete.

A computer is not merely the sum of its utility functions.

It's also an environment for thinking.

A musical instrument changes your relationship with sound. A visualizer changes your relationship with data. A programming language changes how you express processes and structures.

A well-designed personal computer can combine these things into something much more interesting than an electronics multitool.

I don't think DIVINER has solved that problem. Far from it.

Some of its applications are more mature than others. The environmental-sensing functions are experimental. The interface has to coexist with real hardware limitations. There's plenty of room for further optimization, testing, and expansion.

But the underlying idea feels worth pursuing.

What if personal computing stopped being exclusively about convenience?

What if the machine could encourage curiosity instead of constantly trying to eliminate every moment of friction?

Not pointless friction, obviously. Nobody needs their Wi-Fi password entry transformed into an interpretive dance.

But exploratory friction. The kind that makes you notice something, wonder how it works, and follow the question somewhere unexpected.

That's the sort of relationship I want with hardware.

A Small Computer Doesn't Need to Pretend to Be a Large One

The most interesting machines are often the ones that have accepted their limitations.

An old synthesizer doesn't need to reproduce an entire recording studio to be worthwhile.

A Game Boy doesn't need photorealistic graphics to support an extraordinary amount of creativity.

A tiny computer doesn't need to provide a miniature imitation of macOS to become a meaningful personal computing environment.

DIVINER has sixteen applications, but I don't want its future to become a contest to see how many icons can be stuffed into a menu.

I'd rather improve the connections between its existing systems.

Make the audio engines more expressive. Explore better ways of representing wireless activity. Improve CSI experimentation and validation. Make the simulator more useful for testing. Develop the architecture so additional applications can integrate without losing the coherence of the environment.

And yes, probably add a few more deeply unnecessary visual effects.

There are standards to maintain.

The point is not to build the most practical handheld computer in existence.

It's to demonstrate that practical computing and distinctive computing are not mutually exclusive.

You can create a useful diagnostic tool without making it visually miserable.

You can write serious embedded C++ while enjoying an absurd fictional interface.

You can turn an ESP32 into a synthesizer, a network observer, a tiny-web browser, and a peculiar little electronic companion.

A computer is still a remarkably open-ended object if you stop accepting the default assumptions about what it's supposed to be.

DIVINER is one attempt to explore that.

And it's available for anyone curious enough to take it apart.

Get DIVINER

DIVINER is free and open source.

The GitHub repository contains the C++ source, PlatformIO configuration, interface previews, simulator, and firmware distribution.

Download DIVINER and explore the source on GitHub

For project documentation, hardware details, development logs, and updates:

Follow DIVINER on Hackaday.io

If you're running a Cardputer ADV, I'd be especially interested in hardware feedback, bug reports, and experiments with the wireless sensing functions.

And if you're one of those people who thinks software should always have a perfectly ordinary interface, I regret to inform you that the glyphs are staying.

Further Down the Rabbit Hole // numbpilled

DIVINER is part of a wider obsession with embedded systems, unusual hardware, wireless research, and computers that don't need somebody else's cloud account to justify their existence.

If you want to go deeper, I've also published paid technical guides and field manuals through numbpilled on Gumroad.

PHYSICAL AGENTS: Bridging OpenClaw With ESP32 Microcontrollers

A practical guide to connecting AI-agent workflows with physical microcontrollers using WebSocket services, custom device commands, telemetry, and hardware control. For anyone interested in building devices that interact with a larger automation environment instead of living entirely inside their own firmware.

ULTRAWIDEBAND STRIKE: UWB Hacking and Proximity Security

An advanced field manual examining UWB security and proximity systems. A separate research topic from DIVINER's ESP32 Wi-Fi features, but relevant to readers interested in the broader problem of how wireless hardware observes, measures, and trusts the physical world.

Explore the complete numbpilled technical archive

Firmware, experimental hardware, wireless research, security tooling, automation, and other projects from the parts of computing that still have sharp edges.
