articles.title: 98 Calls, 98 Errors, 0 Detections: The Bug My Test Suite Called Green
articles.description: A detector returned None on every call for two full corpus runs, and the test suite reported green...
articles.body_html:
A detector returned None on every call for two full corpus runs, and the test suite reported green the whole time.

Not "it ran and found nothing." It never executed a successful call. Every signal I trusted — green tests, firing detectors, clean telemetry — said fine. The only reason I found it is one line in a summary file I'd been skimming past.

This is the kind of bug except Exception: return None makes possible, and most of us have written that line.

The run that looked great

I was piloting 100 synthetic agent traces through the LLM-augmented detectors in agentwatch — one tool in agentic-suite, a suite of open-source, harness-agnostic security tools for AI agents. The summary came back and it looked genuinely good:

traces_processed: 100
chat_calls: 363
embed_calls: 98
errors: 98
total_tokens: 52,578
json_parse_success: 363
json_parse_fail: 0

363 chat calls. 100% JSON parse success. 52,578 tokens. Detectors firing: hallucination: 98, confusion_pattern: 2, quality_degradation: 1. All sensible numbers.

Then one line: embed_calls: 98, errors: 98.

Every single embedding call failed. And I didn't notice — because the corpus run counts fires, not non-fires. A detector that never fires doesn't show up as "0." It's simply absent. And absent is not zero. Absent means this detector never ran.

This wasn't the first time, either. An earlier run, FT-11b, had 24 embed calls with 24 errors — same 100% failure rate, same invisibility. The bug had been there across two full corpus runs (FT-11b at 25 traces, FT-11d at 100 traces), and between them 122 embed calls had all failed. The error rate was in the telemetry the whole time; it just wasn't in the assertions.

The error was sitting in the logs the entire time:

LLM embed call failed: Error code: 404 - {'error': {'message':
"Model 'all-MiniLM-L6-v2' not found. Available models:
Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct-4bit, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit, Qwen3-8B-4bit,
Qwen3.5-4B-4bit, Qwen3.5-9B-MLX-4bit"}}}

Logged 98 times. The tests passed, so nobody went looking for it.

The code path that made it invisible

The client was written to be resilient — a failed embedding shouldn't crash the pipeline:

async def embed(self, text):
    try:
        resp = await client.embeddings.create(model=self.embed_model, input=text)
        return list(resp.data[0].embedding)
    except Exception as exc:
        self._record_error(start)
        logger.warning("LLM embed call failed: %s", exc)
        return None  # ← silent failure

The detector treats None as "no vector available," which is reasonable:

current_vector = await self._client.embed(output_text)
if current_vector is None:
    return None  # "can't compare vectors → no anomaly"

And the test reads None as "didn't fire," which is correct for a negative case:

fired = anomaly is not None
fire_ok = fired == scenario.expect_fire   # False == False → pass

Three different meanings collapsed into one None:

A None from "I checked and found no anomaly" == a None from "I couldn't check because the API failed" == a None from "I never called the API at all."

Without call telemetry, those are indistinguishable. All three look like a passing negative case.

The reason this stayed hidden in the corpus runs is structural. Those runs count fires. output_drift wasn't "0" in the anomaly counts — it was absent. And absent reads exactly like "the detector ran and found nothing" when you're scanning a summary.

Making the detector actually work

The endpoint had no embedding model at all. OMLX only serves chat completions — all-MiniLM-L6-v2 isn't on the list. So when embed() comes back empty, I now ask the same model to rate how similar two texts are, on a 0-to-1 scale:

if current_vector is not None and baseline is not None:
    sim = cosine_similarity(current_vector, baseline)
else:
    # Embedding unavailable — fall back to chat-based similarity
    sim = await self._chat_similarity(baseline_text, output_text)
distance = 1.0 - sim
if distance >= self._threshold:
    return Anomaly(..., evidence={"method": "chat-fallback", ...})

The prompt is small and strict: "Compare two texts and rate their semantic similarity on a scale of 0.0 to 1.0. Return only JSON: {"similarity": <float>}." The distance is 1.0 - similarity. It's coarser than vector cosine — the model gives you a judgment, not a continuous metric — but it gets the fire-or-don't-fire decision right.

tip: When a primary API is unavailable, a chat-based fallback can produce correct verdicts with the same model. The tradeoff is precision, not correctness. Record the method in the evidence dict so operators know which path produced a given verdict.

There's a subtlety I almost missed. The first call has to set the baseline, so it returns None regardless — same as the vector path. The fallback only kicks in on the second call forward, once there's a baseline text to compare against. Get that ordering wrong and you fire on the very first trace, which is noise.

The check I should have written first

This is the part most suites skip. Before each scenario, snapshot the client's call counters. After, measure the delta for that scenario:

stats_before = dict(client._stats)
anomaly = await det.detect_async(summary, spans, pool=None)
stats_after = dict(client._stats)

llm_calls = stats_after["chat_calls"] - stats_before["chat_calls"]
embed_calls = stats_after["embed_calls"] - stats_before["embed_calls"]
llm_called_ok = (llm_calls + embed_calls) > 0

ok = fire_ok and sev_ok and type_ok and expl_ok and evid_ok and llm_called_ok

If the LLM was never called, the scenario fails — even if the detector returned the "right" answer. A silent None with zero calls is a hidden skip, not a pass.

That check is the difference between a real pass and a hidden skip, and it's the one most suites don't have. It's also cheap: the client already tracks its own call counts for telemetry, so the harness just reads them.

After the fix, both scenarios run with real calls and real evidence:

✅ ED1  output_drift  fire=True   sev=critical  llm_calls=1  llm_errors=2
✅ ED2  output_drift  fire=False  sev=None      llm_calls=1  llm_errors=2

The two llm_errors are the failed embed calls — still 404, still logged, but now they don't define the outcome. The one llm_calls is the chat fallback doing the actual work. The model's actual verdicts:

ED1 (completely different texts):  {"similarity": 0.1}   → distance 0.9 → fires critical
ED2 (nearly identical texts):      {"similarity": 0.95}  → distance 0.05 → silent (correct)

Both were the right call. And this time I can prove the model actually made them.

This isn't about embeddings

The shape repeats anywhere a dependency returns a sentinel on failure:

Dependency Sentinel Looks like
LLM embed() None "no anomaly"
DB fetchrow() None "no baseline"
HTTP GET "" "no data"
Cache get() None "not in cache"
File read() "" "file is empty"

In every case, the failure wears the costume of legitimate emptiness. The test passes. The system is broken. Nobody knows — until someone counts the calls or checks the status, which is the thing the test didn't do.

The fix is always the same shape: prove the dependency was exercised, not just check the output. Count the calls. Check the response status. Assert the network was reached. A None return is only trustworthy if you can prove the call happened.

What I changed

A missing anomaly type is not "zero anomalies." It's "this detector never ran." Check for presence, not just count.

Log warnings are not alerts. The 404 was logged 98 times in one run, 24 in an earlier one, and nobody saw it. If a failure matters, make it an assertion, not a log line.

None is a terrible sentinel because it doesn't tell you which of its three meanings it has. "I checked," "I couldn't check," and "I never tried" all collapse into the same value and the same passing test.

The deeper habit change for me was the assertion. Before this, my tests asked "did the detector return the right answer?" After this, they also ask "did it actually do the work that produces an answer?" The first question can be satisfied by accident. The second one can't.

All of it is fixed in agentwatch v0.1.0, with the llm_called_ok check enforced on every LLM scenario.

The question worth asking of your own repo: which green test would still pass if the service behind it were down? The answer is usually the one that asserts the output but never asserts the dependency ran.

References

  • Release: agentwatch v0.1.0 on GitHub · on PyPI
  • Suite: agentic-suite — the full set of agent-security tools
  • Field test report (defect D-4)
  • Raw LLM I/O: llm-scenario-io.jsonl
  • Harness: scenario_validation.py

articles.title: Why Stacking RAG Tricks Stops Adding Up
articles.description: Every engineering blog post about Retrieval Augmented Generation follows the same script. The team...
articles.body_html:
Every engineering blog post about Retrieval Augmented Generation follows the same script. The team starts with basic dense embeddings, notices bad precision on domain terms, adds BM25 hybrid search, and logs a 15% bump on their test set. Next week someone benchmarks reciprocal rank fusion reranking and gets another 18%. Then comes query expansion via HyDE for another 14%.

On paper, the team is staring at an arithmetic miracle: three separate upgrades that each brought double-digit gains, suggesting a pipeline nearly 50% better than the baseline.

In production, user complaints about hallucinations barely budge, latency triples, and nobody can explain why adding a second retriever made answer quality worse on large corpora.

A research team from IBM and the Weizmann Institute of Science just published empirical proof for why this happens. In their paper, Retrieval Augmented Generation Compositionality (arXiv:2610.29722), researchers Ido Levy, Segev Shlomov, and Leshem Choshen built an open-source evaluation framework named LASAGNA to test whether isolated RAG improvements actually compose.

They evaluated 450 distinct pipeline configurations across eight standard benchmarks on corpora scaling from 5,000 to 200,000 documents. The results should be required reading for anyone managing search infrastructure.

The composition collapse

The headline finding confirms what systems engineers keep rediscovering in production: components in a RAG stack interact destructively.

When three standard retrieval techniques were evaluated individually, their isolated gains predicted a combined improvement of +47% over baseline. When all three were wired together into the same pipeline, the actual measured improvement was +17%.

Almost two-thirds of the expected gains evaporated in composition.

Expected additive gain:  [=============================== +47%]
Actual composed gain:    [=========== +17%]

The reason comes down to noise overlap and rank perturbation. Individual retrieval papers benchmark a specific technique against a clean baseline. In that narrow context, adding semantic query rewrite captures obscure phrasing that lexical search missed. Rerankers then re-order the top chunks to bubble relevant passages to the top.

When you chain them, each stage introduces its own distribution shift:

  1. Query rewriting frequently introduces semantic drift, generating alternative queries that pull adjacent but irrelevant context.
  2. Cross-encoder rerankers, trained on specific passage distributions, spend their scoring budget sorting out distractor passages introduced by the upstream rewriters.
  3. Context compressors clip passages based on isolated token saliency rather than factual cohesion.

By the time the context window reaches the generator, the prompt is packed with high-similarity distractors that look convincing to attention heads but dilute the exact factual anchors the model needs to answer the question.

Retrieval precision fights generator faithfulness

The second finding in the LASAGNA benchmarks is even nastier: retrieval metrics and answer faithfulness frequently optimize in opposite directions.

Most RAG engineering teams use retrieval benchmarks like Recall@K or Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) as primary optimization targets. The assumption is straightforward: if better chunks enter the prompt, the model will output better answers.

Levy, Shlomov, and Choshen found this assumption falls apart when evaluating end-to-end faithfulness. Certain combinations that maximized retrieval recall simultaneously increased factual hallucinations in the generated response.

When a pipeline aggressively packs the context with multiple overlapping chunks to maximize recall, it increases context density. Dense models given three chunks containing slightly conflicting phrasing or temporal mismatch often synthesize plausible-sounding blends rather than grounding on the single authoritative sentence.

If your evaluation suite measures retrieval quality and answer accuracy in separate silos, you will easily deploy configurations that win on search metrics while degrading production reliability.

Corpus scale scrambles the leaderboard

The third insight addresses a subtle trap in developer benchmarks: testing on toy datasets.

In the paper's experiments, the best-performing pipeline configuration on a 5,000-document corpus was routinely overtaken as the corpus expanded to 50,000 and 200,000 documents.

On a 5,000-document corpus, dense vector search handles domain coverage well because the embedding space is relatively sparse. High-dimensional vector collisions are rare, so query augmentation can afford to cast a wide semantic net without drowning the context in false positives.

At 200,000 documents, the dense vector space gets crowded. The number of documents sharing superficial semantic similarity with any given query grows by orders of magnitude. In that environment, aggressive query expansion and broad chunk retrieval flood the candidate pool with high-scoring noise. Techniques that helped at 5K documents actively degrade performance at 200K documents, while stricter lexical filtering and conservative retrieval budgets pull ahead.

If you tune your chunking strategies, top-k parameters, and reranker thresholds against a staging corpus of a few thousand docs, that tuning is practically guaranteed to fail when pointed at your production index.

Testing the full harness

The authors released their testing harness, LASAGNA, specifically to force researchers and builders to test components in context.

The takeaway for anyone running production pipelines is straightforward: stop benchmarking RAG components in isolation.

If you are considering a new embedding model, a fancy query expansion prompt, or a learned reranker, testing it against a standalone retrieval dataset tells you very little about whether your users will get fewer hallucinations.

Measure end-to-end task completion on your actual corpus scale, keep the pipeline as lean as possible, and treat every additional component as an interaction tax until the composed stack proves otherwise.

articles.title: I Allocated 1.5 GB Just to Add Vectors Together
articles.description: C# 14 lets you write your own in-place +=. I used it to fold 200,000 vectors with zero allocations instead of 1.5 GB, and measured the gap.
articles.body_html:
I had a loop that did something embarrassingly simple: fold a stream of feature vectors into one running total. Add a vector, add the next, keep going. A few hundred thousand of them. The math is a for-loop over some doubles, nothing that should trouble the garbage collector.

The allocation profile said otherwise. Gigabytes. For adding numbers.

I knew why the second I looked at the operator. I'd written + the tidy, immutable way years ago and never thought about it again:

public static Vec operator +(Vec a, Vec b)
{
    var result = new double[a.Data.Length];
    for (int i = 0; i < result.Length; i++)
        result[i] = a.Data[i] + b.Data[i];
    return new Vec(result);
}

That's a perfectly reasonable operator. Every call hands back a brand new Vec with its own fresh array, nobody's state gets stomped, and you can reason about it without fear. It's also a fresh 8 KB array on the heap every single time you add two 1024-dimension vectors. In a one-off expression that's free. In a fold over a stream, it's a steady firehose into gen 0.

My accumulation loop was the firehose:

var acc = new Vec(Dims);
for (int i = 0; i < input.Length; i++)
    acc = acc + input[i];

Read that acc = acc + input[i] again. I'm allocating a whole new accumulator on every iteration and throwing the old one away. I never needed a new object. I wanted to pour the next vector into the one I already had.

The operator I couldn't write before

Until C# 14 there was no clean way to say that. += was always just sugar for a = a + b: it called your operator +, took the result, and assigned it back. You couldn't hook the "in place" part because there was no in-place part to hook.

C# 14 adds user-defined compound assignment operators. You write operator += as its own thing. It's an instance method, it returns void, and it mutates this.

public void operator +=(Vec other)
{
    var mine = Data;
    var theirs = other.Data;
    for (int i = 0; i < mine.Length; i++)
        mine[i] += theirs[i];
}

No new. No array. It reaches into the buffer this instance already owns and adds the other vector straight into it. The call site doesn't change at all: acc += input[i] now finds this operator instead of falling back to +. If I hadn't written it, the compiler would've quietly used operator + like always. You only get the new behavior when you opt in.

I counted it

I don't trust "should be faster," so I measured. I built 200,000 vectors of 1024 doubles each, folded them both ways, and tracked wall-clock time (best of five) alongside bytes allocated with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread(). This is a container with workstation GC, not a lab bench, so I care about the ratio and the allocation column, not the exact milliseconds.

dims=1024, vectors=200,000, rounds=5, GC=workstation

acc = acc + v   best    740.0 ms   allocated   1571.7 MB   checksum 102400896.09
acc += v        best    301.9 ms   allocated      0.0 MB   checksum 102400896.09

same result: True
time ratio:  2.45x

1.5 GB versus zero. Same checksum, so the two loops genuinely compute the same answer. The in-place version came out 2.45x faster, and most of that gap isn't the addition. It's the collector cleaning up a gigabyte and a half of short-lived arrays that never had any reason to exist. Zero megabytes still makes me grin a little. The whole fold runs without handing the GC a single byte.

When I'd leave the old operator alone

Here's the part the benchmark won't tell you: mutating in place throws away the one thing immutable + was buying you. With operator +, nobody's vector changes under them. With operator +=, if two references point at the same Vec and one of them does +=, the other just silently got mutated too. That's a classic aliasing bug, and it's exactly the kind of thing that's fine in a tight local loop and nasty in a shared domain model.

So I'm not about to replace every + with an in-place +=. For value-ish types you pass around, compare, and cache, immutability is worth more than the allocations. My honest rule: reach for the in-place operator when you've got a genuine hot accumulation loop and the accumulator is local and yours. Everywhere else, let + keep making new things.

One more sharp edge. The compiler doesn't enforce consistency, so you can define += without +, or make them disagree, and it won't say a word. I'd keep the two in sync regardless, because a += that quietly diverges from + is a debugging session waiting to happen.

I normally drop a link to the runnable sample here, but my code repo push got blocked this time, so the whole thing is right below. Target net10.0 with <LangVersion>14</LangVersion> and it runs as-is:

using System.Diagnostics;

sealed class Vec
{
    public readonly double[] Data;

    public Vec(int dims) => Data = new double[dims];
    public Vec(double[] data) => Data = data;

    // Immutable style: a fresh Vec + array on every add.
    public static Vec operator +(Vec a, Vec b)
    {
        var result = new double[a.Data.Length];
        for (int i = 0; i < result.Length; i++)
            result[i] = a.Data[i] + b.Data[i];
        return new Vec(result);
    }

    // C# 14 in-place compound assignment: mutates this buffer, allocates nothing.
    public void operator +=(Vec other)
    {
        var mine = Data;
        var theirs = other.Data;
        for (int i = 0; i < mine.Length; i++)
            mine[i] += theirs[i];
    }

    public double Checksum()
    {
        double s = 0;
        foreach (var d in Data) s += d;
        return s;
    }
}

static class Program
{
    const int Dims = 1024;
    const int Count = 200_000;
    const int Rounds = 5;

    static Vec[] BuildInputs()
    {
        var rng = new Random(42);
        var vecs = new Vec[Count];
        for (int i = 0; i < Count; i++)
        {
            var d = new double[Dims];
            for (int j = 0; j < Dims; j++) d[j] = rng.NextDouble();
            vecs[i] = new Vec(d);
        }
        return vecs;
    }

    static (double sum, long bytes, double ms) RunPlus(Vec[] input)
    {
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        var acc = new Vec(Dims);
        for (int i = 0; i < input.Length; i++)
            acc = acc + input[i];
        long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        sw.Stop();
        return (acc.Checksum(), after - before, sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
    }

    static (double sum, long bytes, double ms) RunCompound(Vec[] input)
    {
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        var acc = new Vec(Dims);
        for (int i = 0; i < input.Length; i++)
            acc += input[i];
        long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        sw.Stop();
        return (acc.Checksum(), after - before, sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);
    }

    static void Main()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"dims={Dims}, vectors={Count:N0}, rounds={Rounds}, GC=workstation");
        var input = BuildInputs();

        _ = RunPlus(input);      // warm up the JIT
        _ = RunCompound(input);

        double plusChk = 0, compChk = 0, plusBest = double.MaxValue, compBest = double.MaxValue;
        long plusBytes = 0, compBytes = 0;

        for (int r = 0; r < Rounds; r++)
        {
            var p = RunPlus(input);
            var c = RunCompound(input);
            plusChk = p.sum; compChk = c.sum;
            plusBytes = p.bytes; compBytes = c.bytes;
            if (p.ms < plusBest) plusBest = p.ms;
            if (c.ms < compBest) compBest = c.ms;
        }

        Console.WriteLine($"acc = acc + v   best {plusBest,8:F1} ms   allocated {plusBytes / (1024.0 * 1024.0),8:F1} MB   checksum {plusChk:F2}");
        Console.WriteLine($"acc += v        best {compBest,8:F1} ms   allocated {compBytes / (1024.0 * 1024.0),8:F1} MB   checksum {compChk:F2}");
        Console.WriteLine($"same result: {Math.Abs(plusChk - compChk) < 1e-6}");
        Console.WriteLine($"time ratio:  {plusBest / compBest:F2}x");
    }
}

Have you hit a spot where += was quietly allocating behind your back? I'd like to hear where it bit you.

— still benchmarking things nobody asked me to benchmark

articles.title: 🔢 The JSON Numbers JavaScript Quietly Corrupts
articles.description: JSON.parse changes your data and never says so. Three distinct failure modes, only one of which is the famous one about large integers.
articles.body_html:
Overview

This post will help identify the ways JSON.parse silently changes your data, and what you can do about it. We will cover why it happens, the three distinct failure modes it produces, how to check whether your own pipeline is affected, and the approach I use in my own tooling to prevent it. Each failure mode includes an example you can run in your browser console right now.

💡 Every example in this post takes less than ten seconds to verify. Open your console and follow along.

📚 Table of Contents

  • Why it happens
  • The three ways it bites
    • Large integers round
    • Overflow becomes null
    • Formatting is destroyed even when the value survives
  • What most tools do about it
  • What we do in Prettify
  • How to check whether this affects you
  • Drawbacks
  • The short version

First, try it yourself

Paste this into a browser console:

JSON.parse('{"id": 9007199254740993}').id

You get 9007199254740992. Off by one. No error, no warning, no truncation notice. The value you asked for is gone and something that looks just like it is standing where it was.

This is not a bug in JSON.parse. It is doing what the spec says. But it means that any JavaScript program that reads JSON, touches it, and writes it back is a program that can silently change your data, and most of them do not know it.

Why it happens

JSON has one numeric type and no size limit. The grammar is happy to describe a four-hundred-digit integer.

JavaScript also has one numeric type: the IEEE-754 double. It has 53 bits of integer precision. Past Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, which is 9007199254740991, consecutive integers stop being representable, and the parser rounds to whatever double is nearest.

So JSON.parse maps an unbounded numeric grammar onto a bounded numeric type. There is no way to do that without losing something, and the standard's choice is to lose it silently.

The three ways it bites

Value loss is the famous one. It is not the only one, and it is not the most common.

1. Large integers round 

JSON.parse('{"id": 1071004833782874112}').id
// 1071004833782874100

The last two digits are invented. That is a Discord-style snowflake ID, and the same applies to Twitter/X IDs, most database bigints, Stripe-style numeric identifiers, and anything else that packs a timestamp into a 64-bit integer.

🚧 The insidious part is that IDs are exactly the values where a near-miss is worse than a crash. A rounded price is obviously wrong. A rounded ID is a valid-looking ID that points at nothing, or worse, at something else.

2. Overflow becomes null 

JSON.parse('{"v": 1e400}').v
// Infinity

JSON.stringify(Infinity)
// "null"

Read a number too large for a double and you get Infinity. Write it back out and JSON.stringify turns Infinity into null, because JSON has no infinity literal.

So a round trip converts a number into a null. Downstream, that is not a precision problem. It is a type change, and whatever consumes the field next is going to be surprised.

3. Formatting is destroyed even when the value survives 

JSON.stringify(JSON.parse('{"v": 4.0}'))
// {"v":4}

4.0 and 4 are the same number. They are not the same document.

If you are round-tripping a config file, a fixture, an API contract, or anything a human wrote and will read again, 4.0 becoming 4 is a diff. It shows up in code review. It shows up in a git blame. Version-controlled JSON that a formatter "cleaned" is a classic source of noise commits.

The same goes for 1.00, -0 becoming 0, and 5e+3 becoming 5000.

And all three are silent

Nothing throws. Nothing logs. The document parses, the program runs, and the tests pass because the fixtures were generated by the same broken round trip.

You find out when a customer reports that a record will not load, and the ID in your logs is one digit off from the ID in theirs.

What most tools do about it

Nothing, mostly.

Every JSON formatter, viewer, and prettifier that works by calling JSON.parse and then JSON.stringify has all of these behaviors. That is the standard implementation. Paste a Discord message dump into a random online JSON formatter and the IDs come back wrong.

The workarounds people reach for:

  • Parse to BigInt. Handles large integers, does nothing for 4.0 or 1e400, and gives you a type that will not JSON.stringify without a custom replacer.
  • Parse numbers as strings. Safe, and it breaks every consumer that expected a number.
  • Ask the API for string IDs. Correct, and most public APIs already do this for exactly this reason. Also not available to you when you are just looking at somebody else's payload.

What we do in Prettify

The rule is: preserve the token, not the value.

When parsing, each numeric token gets one question asked about it. Would writing this back out produce the exact bytes I read? If yes, it stays an ordinary JavaScript number. If no, it becomes a wrapper that holds the original digit string.

The wrapper type and the two helpers below come from lossless-json. The policy around them is ours, and it is the part worth copying.

function parseNumber(value: string): number | LosslessNumber {
  if (isSafeNumber(value) && String(parseFloat(value)) === value) {
    return parseFloat(value)
  }
  return parseLosslessNumber(value)
}

Two conditions, because there are two independent failure modes, and this is the part that most implementations miss.

isSafeNumber catches value loss. It does not catch formatting loss: it says 4.0 is perfectly safe, because numerically it is. 4.0 and 4 are the same double.

That is why the second check exists. String(parseFloat("4.0")) is "4", which is not "4.0", so the token gets preserved even though nothing about its value was ever at risk.

💡 Checking only isSafeNumber is the natural implementation, and it silently reformats your document.

Wrap only what needs wrapping

The other half of the design is that most numbers are not wrapped. 1, 42, 0.1, -17.5 all stay ordinary numbers, because they round-trip exactly. Only the tokens that would change get the wrapper.

This matters for a reason that is more practical than philosophical: a wrapper is typeof === 'object'. Every typeof x === 'number' check in the codebase is false for it, and every "is this a container?" check is true for it unless you exclude it. Wrapping everything would mean auditing every numeric code path in the application. Wrapping only unsafe tokens keeps the blast radius to the small set of documents that actually contain them.

Viewing is not computing

Preserving a number exactly and doing arithmetic on it are incompatible goals in a language with one float type. So the two are separated by policy:

  • View, select, copy, round-trip: exact. The digits you pasted are the digits you get back.
  • Compute: coerced, and you are told. Arithmetic, aggregation, and comparison flatten to a float, because they have to. When that happens, the app says so.

That last clause is the whole point. The original sin of JSON.parse is not that it loses precision. It is that it loses precision without mentioning it. An answer you know is approximate is a usable answer. An answer you believe is exact and is not is a landmine.

How to check whether this affects you

Fastest test, in any JavaScript runtime:

const original = yourJsonString
const roundTripped = JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(original))
// If these differ, your pipeline is changing documents.

That catches all three cases at once, formatting included.

If it comes back different, the questions worth asking are: does anything downstream compare these documents, diff them, sign them, hash them, or use a numeric field as a key? If yes, you have a real problem rather than a cosmetic one.

Drawbacks

Being honest about the limits of this approach:

  • It only covers JSON and JSONL. The policy above applies to Prettify's JSON pipeline. YAML and CSV go through their own parsers and get ordinary JavaScript numbers, with all three behaviors described in this post.
  • Computing still coerces. Preserving a number exactly and doing math on it are incompatible in JavaScript. Arithmetic flattens to a float. The best a tool can do is tell you when it happened.
  • It does not help with data that was already corrupted upstream. If the ID was rounded before it reached you, no parser can recover the digits that were lost.

The short version

  • JSON.parse silently rounds integers past 9007199254740991
  • 1e400 round-trips to null, changing the type
  • 4.0 round-trips to 4, changing the document
  • None of it warns you
  • The fix is to preserve the original token when re-serializing it would differ, and to check formatting as well as value

Prettify preserves these numbers byte for byte, in JSON and JSONL, in the browser: paste a payload with a snowflake ID into the JSON viewer and the digits come back unchanged. The jq engine applies the same policy, and flags any query that had to coerce.

Happy Coding 🚀

Blog Post: https://prettify.tools/blog/the-json-numbers-javascript-corrupts

If you liked this content, follow me on Twitter @alexi_be3 💙

articles.body_html:
I wrote four security findings against a 47-line Node service. Two of them were false. One cites a file that does not exist.

Cloudflare's findings validator passed all four.

That is not a bug in the validator. It is the clearest way I found to show where the value of an AI security review actually sits.

The skill

cloudflare/security-audit-skill is a coding-agent skill that turns one agent into a coordinator of many: recon agents map the code, hunter agents look for bugs, and fresh verifier agents try to knock each finding down before it reaches a report. It was on GitHub trending this week with almost 2,000 stars in a day, 35,690 in total when I checked. MIT licensed. Cloudflare says it is the starting point of the vulnerability harness they now run across their whole fleet.

I measured it before reading it closely. The skill is 15 markdown files: 1,778 lines, 24,768 words, about 183 KB. At the usual four bytes per token that is roughly 46,000 tokens of instructions, loaded in pieces as a run needs them. Cloudflare's blog post says the first version was about 450 lines.

Two zero-dependency Node scripts sit beside the prose: validate-findings.cjs (773 lines) and validate-coverage-ledger.cjs (872 lines). Their own test suites ran clean on my machine, 34 and 31 tests.

The part that caught my eye is the proportion. Of the six phases, two exist only to disprove: Phase 3 hands every candidate to a fresh agent told to refute it, and Phase 5 sends another fresh agent over the final record (the quick profile merges the two). Each Phase 3 verifier prompt carries about 17.5 KB of fixed text before it sees the candidate: a six-step refutation prompt, a file-promotion procedure, and three schema branches copied in verbatim.

What I actually did

I did not install the skill, and no agent ran it. The README's install path is a skills CLI that writes into your agent's config, and I don't do that for a post.

Instead I wrote a small target, played the hunter by hand, and ran the skill's real validator on the result. The target is a notes service on node:http and node:sqlite with dummy users alice and bob. These are the two functions that matter:

function search(user, q) {
  const sql = "SELECT id, title FROM notes WHERE owner = '" + user + "' AND title LIKE '%" + q + "%'";
  return db.prepare(sql).all();
}

function getNote(user, id) {
  return db.prepare('SELECT id, title, body FROM notes WHERE id = ? AND owner = ?').get(id, user);
}

There is also an /admin/export route gated on X-Forwarded-For starting with 10..

Then I wrote four findings the way a hunter returns them, in the skill's schema:

  1. SQL injection in search. Real.
  2. SQL injection in getNote, marked confirmed, with an observed result claiming it returned bob's note. False.
  3. SQL injection in findUser at src/users.js line 212. Invented: that file does not exist.
  4. The export gate trusts a header a client can set, unless a proxy rewrites it. A real question, but the proxy is not in the repo.

What the validator checks 

$ node validate-findings.cjs proposed.json
PASS: 4 findings valid

To be fair to it, it does enforce the contract. When I raised one record's overall severity above its impact, or put a severity on the needs_validation record, it failed, with exact paths. It checks shape, ordering, safe relative paths, and that a confirmed record has an observed result written in visible text.

It never opens a source file. It doesn't take the target path at all. The skill says this itself, in one line of Phase 4: validator success "proves format and ledger consistency only." A hunter's observed result is a string, and my invented one was schema-valid.

A cheap check gets one

Next I wrote 15 lines of Node that open every cited file and check the line exists:

ok   admin/export-xff-gate
ok   notes/note-sql-concat
ok   notes/search-sql-concat
FAIL users/find-user-template-sql  src/routes/login.js: no such file; src/users.js: no such file

That kills the invented file. Cloudflare's harness has the same idea in plain code: per the blog, deterministic code confirms the cited files and paths exist before a finding moves on.

It does nothing for the getNote claim. Line 24 is real, and it really runs a query with the id in it. Every fact the record cites is true except the one that matters.

The skeptic gets the rest

So I walked the Phase 3 prompt by hand. Step 2 says to rebuild the strongest control on the path. For getNote that takes one read: id and owner are bound as placeholders. Step 3 says to reproduce the minimum result yourself. My service is my own code with dummy data, so I ran it on loopback (the skill demands an OS-enforced sandbox before it runs anyone else's target; this was not that). Output trimmed:

search, normal     200 [{"id":1,"title":"groceries"}]
search, payload    200 [{"id":1,"title":"groceries"},{"id":2,"title":"payroll"}]
note, bob id       200 null
note, payload      200 null
note, payload 2    200 null
export, XFF 10.    200 [... both users' notes ...]

The search payload ' OR 1=1 -- hands alice the title of bob's note. Every getNote payload returns nothing. The export gate opens to a header alone, but whether a client can send that header in production depends on a proxy the repo doesn't contain, so it stays needs_validation with an owner check attached. That is the skill's rule for a deployment fact, and I agree with it.

The final file: one confirmed, one needs validation, two rejected.

$ node validate-findings.cjs findings.json
PASS: 4 findings valid

Same validator, same four fingerprints, same PASS. In between, two of the three "confirmed" bugs became rejected. Only reading the code at the cited line and running the payload told the files apart.

Why the skeptic is the expensive part

Finding candidates is cheap now. Cloudflare's blog reports 20,799 raw candidates from their discovery harness, of which about 12,057 survived validation, and an early validation rejection rate of 40% before better recon brought it down to 11%. At 40%, a team without a refuter gets four bad tickets in every ten. Somebody pays for those, and it's usually a maintainer.

That is also the theme of OpenAI's "Patch the Planet" post on coordinating disclosure as agents surface critical bugs, which was on the Hacker News front page the same day.

So my claim: when you judge an AI security tool, judge the step that tries to prove the finding wrong. The hunt is a hypothesis generator. The product is the record that survived.

Where it falls short

Cost is real. In the Hacker News thread, jesse_dot_id reported at least 150k tokens on a fairly small FastAPI project before hitting a session limit. Issue #20 is a blind test on one seeded target, three rounds per arm, by a team with its own competing tool, which it discloses. There the quick profile cost a median $29.95 against $2.06 for one plain agent, and found the same share of the seeded bugs (a median recall of 0.467 for both). On a small, clean target the skeptic may have nothing to kill.

And a skeptic that shares the hunter's model is not fully independent. Per that same issue, the skill's verifiers inherit the session's model. Cloudflare's own pipeline triages with a different model from the one that hunts. Fresh context is not a different mind.

If you run AI reviews on your code today, what does the step that tries to disprove a finding look like: a second model, a test that must fail before the fix, or you?

articles.title: Give Your AI Feature a Kill Switch, a Budget, and a Paper Trail
articles.description: The second-most dangerous demo is "watch the agent do everything." The most dangerous is shipping...
articles.body_html:
The second-most dangerous demo is "watch the agent do everything." The most dangerous is shipping that demo to real users on Monday.

I build web and mobile products with Node, React, and Flutter, and I speak about AI in community spaces. The pattern I keep seeing: teams add a chat box or an "AI assistant" tab, wire an API key, and hope prompt vibes will behave in production. Hope is not an architecture.

This post is a practical starter kit for fullstack builders: three controls every AI feature should have before you invite non-technical users — a kill switch, a budget, and a paper trail. No cloud-vendor lock-in assumed. You can implement these with boring Node middleware and a small React admin panel.

Why demos lie

Figure: gate every model call — kill switch, budget, paper trail.

In a Meetup demo:

  • You are the only user
  • You type polite, on-distribution prompts
  • You ignore the bill
  • You can Ctrl+C when it loops
  • Nobody pastes a 40-page PDF of junk to "summarize"

In production:

  • Users paste secrets by accident
  • Prompts go adversarial or just confused
  • A retry storm turns into a surprise invoice
  • An agent tool call hits the wrong environment
  • You need to explain what happened three days later

Governance sounds enterprise. The core is simpler: assume the model will be wrong, expensive, or both — and design the blast radius.

Control 1: Kill switch (feature flags that actually stop spend)

A kill switch is not a blog toggle in Notion. It is a runtime gate checked before every model call and every tool invocation.

Minimal shape:

// lib/aiFlags.js
export async function assertAiEnabled(featureKey) {
  const row = await db.flags.get(featureKey);
  if (!row?.enabled) {
    const err = new Error("AI_FEATURE_DISABLED");
    err.code = "AI_FEATURE_DISABLED";
    throw err;
  }
}

Call it at the edge of your AI service:

export async function runAssistant({ userId, featureKey, input }) {
  await assertAiEnabled(featureKey);
  // ... budget check, then model call
}

Wire a React admin (or even a secured POST /admin/flags) so you can disable meetup-copilot without redeploying. When something smells wrong at 1 a.m., you want a button — not a pipeline.

Mobile note: Flutter clients should treat AI_FEATURE_DISABLED as a first-class UI state ("Assistant temporarily off"), not a generic 500. Users forgive maintenance; they do not forgive spinning forever.

Bonus: scoped kills

Prefer per-feature flags over a global "AI off":

  • chat.summarize
  • chat.reply-suggest
  • agent.tools.github (keep this off until you are truly ready)

That way a broken experimental agent does not take down a simple title-rewriter that still helps organizers.

Control 2: Budget (tokens, calls, and blast radius)

If you cannot answer "what is the max this feature can cost today?", you do not have a product — you have an open tab.

Soft limits per user / per org 

export async function assertWithinBudget({ tenantId, featureKey }) {
  const usage = await db.usage.today(tenantId, featureKey);
  const limit = await db.limits.get(tenantId, featureKey);

  if (usage.calls >= limit.maxCalls || usage.tokens >= limit.maxTokens) {
    const err = new Error("AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED");
    err.code = "AI_BUDGET_EXCEEDED";
    throw err;
  }
}

Practical defaults for an early community product:

  • Cap calls per user per day
  • Cap max input characters (reject the 2MB paste early)
  • Cap max tool iterations for agents (e.g. 5 steps, then stop with a clear message)
  • Separate "playground" keys from "production" keys

Hard limits at the provider

Also set provider-side spending caps where they exist. Application budgets fail closed when Redis hiccups; provider caps fail closed when your app has a bug. Use both.

Agents need step budgets, not vibes

If you are building anything agent-like (tool calling, multi-step plans):

  • Maximum steps
  • Maximum wall-clock time
  • Allowlist of tools (read calendar ✗ delete calendar until proven)
  • Human confirmation for irreversible actions

Pausing / resuming agents is a hot topic for a reason: long-running autonomy without checkpoints is how you get surprise side effects. Even a simple job table with status: running | paused | done | failed beats an unbounded while-loop in memory.

Control 3: Paper trail (logs you can defend)

When someone asks "why did the assistant tell my users X?", screenshots are not enough.

Log structured events:

await db.aiEvents.insert({
  id: crypto.randomUUID(),
  tenantId,
  userId,
  featureKey,
  model,
  promptVersion,      // e.g. "rsvp-helper@3"
  inputHash,          // hash raw input; store raw only if policy allows
  toolCalls: [...],   // names + args summaries
  outputHash,
  tokensIn,
  tokensOut,
  latencyMs,
  createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
});

Privacy-aware defaults

  • Prefer hashes + short redacted previews over full prompts for sensitive products
  • Never log API keys, auth headers, or payment fields
  • Define retention (30/90 days) and stick to it
  • Make "export my AI history / delete my AI history" a real endpoint if you serve EU users or simply respect people

Prompt versioning is underrated

Store prompts in git (prompts/rsvp-helper.v3.md) and send promptVersion with every call. When behavior changes, you can diff. "The model got dumber" is often "we edited the prompt on Tuesday and forgot."

A thin React admin that earns its keep

You do not need a full observability suite on day one. A single authenticated page with:

  • Feature flags table + toggle
  • Today's spend / call counts per feature
  • Last 50 AI events (status, latency, error code)
  • Big red "disable all AI features" button

…will save you more pain than another model provider abstraction.

How this maps to a real feature

Suppose you add "Suggest event description" for organizers:

  1. Flag: events.ai.suggest-description (default off in prod until soak test)
  2. Budget: 20 suggestions / organizer / day, 1k max input chars
  3. Paper trail: prompt version + hashes + tokens
  4. UX: show the suggestion as a diff the human must accept — never auto-publish
  5. Kill: if suggestions degrade, flip the flag; the rest of the app keeps working

That is product engineering. The model is a dependency, not the product.

Takeaways

  1. Kill switches belong in the request path, not in a document.
  2. Budgets need daily caps, input caps, and agent step caps — plus provider hard limits.
  3. Paper trails need structured events, prompt versions, and privacy rules.
  4. Human confirmation for irreversible actions is not optional.
  5. Ship AI as a flaggable slice of a working app, not as the app's only spine.

If you are adding your first assistant to a Node/React or Flutter app, start with these three controls before you polish the avatar animation. Cool UI with no blast-radius design is how demos become incidents.

What control do you wish you had added earlier — flag, budget, or audit log? I am curious what broke first for other builders.

articles.title: A wrong "closed" never comes back: measuring a job-posting liveness checker on real pages
articles.description: What I found in career-ops's liveness checker over 16 merged PRs, how I measured each fix on real job pages, and what it taught me about permanent decisions.
articles.body_html:
career-ops is an open-source job-search pipeline: Node.js scripts driven by AI coding CLIs, with about 76k stars on GitHub. Before it adds a posting to your pipeline, scan --verify checks that the posting is still open. Where the job board has a public API, it asks the API. Otherwise it loads the page in a headless browser and reads it.

A "closed" or "blocked" verdict goes into your scan history for good, and that posting is skipped on every later scan. So the two ways to be wrong cost very different amounts. A wrong "open" costs one more check later. A wrong "closed" makes a live job disappear from your search without a trace.

Between 3 and 20 October 2026 I had 16 pull requests merged into career-ops, most of them in this liveness checker. This is what I found, how I measured it, and what the fixes look like.

How I found the bugs

The board was busy: 135 open PRs and 208 open issues on 11 October. The project's CONTRIBUTING lets bug fixes go in without an issue, so instead of competing for claimed issues I read modules nobody was working on. I started with the ATS keyword and CV skill checks, which are close to my NLP background, then moved to the liveness checker.

For the checker, I ran it on real postings and read every disagreement. The sources were public job-postings datasets (LinkedIn, USAJOBS) and live boards without an API. Several fixes also came out of the project's own conversations: a merge note from the maintainer, a follow-up the review bot offered, and three follow-ups from my reviews of other contributors' PRs.

A blocked tracker took the whole page down

Many people run a DNS filter that blocks ads and trackers: Pi-hole, AdGuard DNS, Control D, a hosts-file blocklist. Such a filter answers 0.0.0.0 for a tracker it blocks.

The browser check has a security guard that refuses requests to private network addresses, and 0.0.0.0 is on its list. Refusing the tracker is right. But the guard also marked the whole page "blocked", which scan --verify records permanently.

I found it while reviewing another contributor's PR that touches how the guard handles DNS answers. To measure it, I took 35 postings on 19 boards with no API, all live the day before, and checked each one with main's code and with the fix, behind two real filtering resolvers and with no filter as a control:

  • On main, 12 postings behind AdGuard DNS and 20 behind Control D read "blocked".
  • With the fix, none did. Behind Control D, 11 of those 20 read active with a visible Apply button.
  • With no filter, both versions agreed on 32 of 35. The 3 differences were flaky page loads, in both directions.

The fix (#5015) leaves the guard's decision alone. The request is still refused, with the same error. The guard only tags the refusal when the only private addresses in the answer are the filter's:

  if (blocked.length > 0) {
    const denied = new Error(`Access denied: Egress guard blocked private target IP ${blocked[0].ip}`);
    if (blocked.every(({ hit }) => SINKHOLE_ADDRESSES.has(hit))) denied.livenessCode = 'dns_sinkhole';
    throw denied;
  }

A tagged refusal of a tracker, a script or an image no longer decides the page's verdict. Any other private address still counts, even next to 0.0.0.0. I rejected the simpler option, ignoring every private answer for subresources, because it would drop the guard's signal on a host that really resolves into a private network.

The follow-up, #5075, covers the posting's own host. When that host had no usable address, the guard reported "blocked". But no address is often about the run, not the posting: a DNS outage during the scan, or the user's own filter blocking the job board. Now it reads uncertain, and the posting is kept for another check. With the posting's own host failing DNS, 19 of 19 postings from 19 boards were dropped permanently on main, and 19 of 19 were kept with the fix.

The PR states the trade-off: a domain that is really gone now reads uncertain too, because one failed lookup can't tell a dead domain from an outage. A kept dead posting costs one more check later. A pinned live one never comes back.

One failed load failed the rest of the run

This one turned up while I was measuring another fix: a posting whose host no longer resolved broke the checks after it in the same run. I reproduced it on the code from before my DNS change, to rule that out, and traced it to the browser library the next day.

The checker runs every browser check in one tab. When a page fails to load (its host has no address, its certificate has expired, its connection is reset), the browser shows its error page a moment after the checker has moved on, and that interrupts the next page load. The interrupted page then finishes loading late and interrupts the one after it, often to the end of the run. Those checks fail as load errors, so scan --verify keeps the postings without having checked them, and the closed ones among them go into the user's pipeline. The root is a known Playwright issue (microsoft/playwright#35944, closed upstream without a fix).

Through the real CLI, on one list of 45 URLs with 6 failing loads spread among 39 postings that were live the day before:

  • On main, 39 of 39 postings read as load errors, from the first URL to the last.
  • With the fix, none did: 30 active, 1 expired (HTTP 404), 6 "no Apply control", 1 Cloudflare challenge and 1 timeout.

Over 36 failed loads, the browser's error page landed 1 to 69 ms after the failure was reported, median 4 ms. So the fix (#5299) waits for the browser's own signal instead of a fixed delay, for at most 2 s:

async function navigateSettled(page, navigate) {
  try {
    return await navigate();
  } catch (err) {
    const canWait = typeof page.waitForEvent === 'function' && typeof page.mainFrame === 'function';
    if (canWait && err?.name !== 'TimeoutError') {
      await page
        .waitForEvent('framenavigated', {
          predicate: (frame) => frame === page.mainFrame() && frame.url().startsWith('chrome-error:'),
          timeout: FAILED_NAVIGATION_COMMIT_MS,
        })
        .catch(() => {});
    }
    throw err;
  }
}

A timeout is left alone: a timed-out load shows no error page, and the next load cancels it, so waiting would only add 2 s. I rejected parking the tab on a blank page after a failure, which another part of the code does after a search, because that load is interrupted the same way. The review bot pointed out that the old page changing its own address could end the wait too early. I couldn't make that happen in real Chromium in 26 tries, but fixed it anyway, with a test the first version fails.

CI installs no browser, so the tests use a stand-in page that plays out the browser's order of events. The same sequences also run on real Chromium where it can launch.

A ground truth showed a case the issue had missed

I filed #4832 for live postings on seven non-English boards that read as having no Apply button. getManfred, a Spanish tech-job board, was one. Its Apply button says "¡Apúntame!" ("sign me up"), which the checker didn't know, so every live posting read "no Apply control".

getManfred's own feed marks every offer open or closed, so the A/B could measure against the board instead of against my reading of pages. The first run showed a case the issue had missed: one closed posting read open on both versions. Closed postings written in English often have an FAQ button such as "Can I apply if I live outside Spain?", and the English Apply pattern took it for an Apply button.

The page does say the offer is closed, but that sentence renders near the bottom, after the checker's first look on some pages. Above the title, from the start, a closed posting says when it closed ("Oferta cerrada el 27/07/2023"). Closing patterns are read before the Apply button, so an FAQ button can't outvote the date. The fix (#5350) is two patterns:

  /\boferta cerrada el \d{1,2}\/\d{1,2}\/\d{4}/i,  // a closing pattern, read before the Apply button
  /\bapuntame\b/i,                                // an Apply label, accent-free like the others

I left out the verb "aplicar": 73 of the 111 getManfred pages I measured have an FAQ button that uses it, closed ones included. On 136 real page loads:

  • Live: all 28 open offers read active with the fix. On main, 25 read "no Apply control", and the other 3 read active only through their FAQ button.
  • Closed: all 83 read closed with the fix. On main, 17 read active, all of them written in English and read through the FAQ button.

The board already knew the answer

No Fluff Jobs, a Polish tech-job board, was the last of my board families from #4832, and the checker read it backwards. A live posting puts its Apply button ("Aplikuj") inside a page header, which the checker skips as page chrome, so every live posting read "no Apply control". A closed posting moves to a search page with a promo link that also says "Aplikuj", so most closed postings read as open.

I'd planned label patterns. Then I found that the board's per-posting API says directly whether a posting is open. So the fix (#5428) is an API rung, as several other boards already have. The API answers "published" (open), "expired" (closed) or "does not exist". A status the rung doesn't know reads uncertain, never closed, and an answer it can't read falls back to the browser.

Through the real CLI on 102 postings (40 live from the board's search API, 59 closed from Wayback Machine archives, 1 gone and 2 made up):

  • On main, all 40 live postings read "no Apply control", and 42 of the 59 closed ones read active.
  • With the fix, 40 of 40 read active and 59 of 59 read closed, without opening a browser: 26 s against 348 s.

The review bot raised two valid points on it. I measured that they change no verdict on today's API answers and shipped them as a follow-up, #5533.

VDAB, the job board of Flanders' public employment service, looks like the second case. A closed vacancy there keeps its page and its Apply button, and only a banner says it's closed. Reading the page while it renders, main read 13 of 84 loads of closed vacancies as open. My open PR, #5703, asks VDAB's per-vacancy API, which the page itself uses. One choice in it is deliberate: a "pending" vacancy reads uncertain, not closed, because one pending vacancy had never been published at all, and a closed verdict is recorded for good.

How each fix was tested

Every PR adds tests that fail on main and pass with the fix. I checked each one with mutation variants: deliberately broken versions of the fix that the tests must catch. On #4810, 13 of 13 were caught; on #4833, 12 of 12. I also ran the full suite on each branch against main. Over three weeks it grew from about 11,600 to about 16,800 tests.

Among the things the maintainer's merge notes thanked were the edge-case tests: in the keyword check, the ones that keep "IT", "HR" and "AWS" from matching ordinary words; in the checker, the one for a button that is hidden or sits in the navigation.

The rest of the work

  • Four fixes to the ATS keyword-coverage and CV skill-gap checks. The keyword check, for one, looked for a single English heading, so reports in the translated modes stopped with an error. Here is the same report under each mode's heading on main, from #4725: 
  en  ## Keywords extracted         exit 0  coverage 80%
  de  ## Extrahierte Keywords       exit 1  No "## Keywords extracted" block found (or it is empty).
  es  ## Palabras clave extraídas   exit 1  same
  ko  ## 추출한 키워드              exit 1  same
  zh  ## ATS 关键词提取             exit 1  same

On the branch, all five exit 0 at 80%.

  • One fix to the Gupy provider, whose API had moved to another host. It closed #4831, which I filed.
  • Reviews of five other contributors' liveness and scan PRs, all merged. Four authors applied my findings or suggested tests before merge, and a fifth took my suggestion into a new version.
  • #4832 is closed: every board in it has a merged fix. We split it by approach instead of racing. The contributor who wrote the providers for its Chinese boards moved them to per-posting APIs, another contributor took CareerViet, and I did the Dutch boards, getManfred and No Fluff Jobs.

Three more PRs are open: #5535 (HiringRoom's "Postularse" label, approved), #5691 (Tech in Asia's Apply link in the page header) and #5703 (VDAB's API). Since 9 October I've been on the project's contributors team. Thanks to the maintainer for quick merges and for merge notes that say exactly what they valued.

What I learned

  • Mistakes aren't symmetric when a pipeline makes permanent decisions. A false "open" costs one more check later. A false "closed" can't be undone. Most of my liveness fixes move an unsure case from permanent to retry-next-time.
  • Find a ground truth before trusting an A/B. getManfred's feed and VDAB's API measured the fixes, not my reading of pages. getManfred's feed also showed a case the issue had missed.
  • Look for the board's own API before patching the page reader. No Fluff Jobs looked like a label-and-pattern job. Its API answered both sides directly, needed no browser, and left the rules every board shares untouched.
  • Measure before changing a rule every board shares. The header skip looked like a bug on every board, but 821 real pages from 268 sites showed it hid only one board's Apply button. So #5691 (open) reads one narrow case, a link to the posting's own page, instead of every button in every header.
  • Separate the change from the page. Live pages differ from one load to the next, so two runs can disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with the code. Running both versions on the same loaded page at the same moment settles it: on #5691's control pages, all 5 verdict differences came with identical button lists.
  • Some bugs live between two systems. The failed-load chain came from the browser and its automation library disagreeing about when a failed load is over. Waiting for the browser's own signal stops the chain, at a cost of a few milliseconds per failed load.
  • Reviews count as contributions. Reviewing another contributor's DNS change led straight to the bug #5015 fixes.

All 16 merged PRs: https://github.com/career-ops-hq/career-ops/pulls?q=is%3Apr+is%3Amerged+author%3Aroydonsequeira

articles.title: Apple took a bite out of theirs, so I made the whole apple: Bezel, open-source clock, calendar and weather web components (no dependencies, ~25 kB)
articles.description: Bezel is a set of five web components inspired by Apple's StandBy widgets, with my own stamp on...
articles.body_html:
Bezel is a set of five web components inspired by Apple's StandBy widgets, with my own stamp on them. Unlike the originals, they run anywhere, not just on Apple devices.

  • Clock (three faces, optional second time zone)
  • Calendar
  • Weather (live from Open-Meteo, no API key)
  • Glance (date, clock, weather and today's agenda from an .ics feed)
  • Poster (a month in huge type)

Usage is one script tag plus an element:

<script type="module" src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ShazMoghaddam/bezel@v2.0.0/dist/bezel.min.js"></script>
<bezel-clock variant="relief" theme="ember"></bezel-clock>

Some technical bits that might be interesting:

  • Everything is sized in container query units, so one stylesheet works from 120 px to 4K with no breakpoints
  • Dark mode is a chain of CSS var() fallbacks: your dark colour, then the dark theme, then the normal colour
  • The weather sky is SVG with gradients rather than blurred CSS, and rain/snow are SVG patterns that loop seamlessly
  • All tiles on a page share one timer and pause when off screen
  • When you round the corners, a single calculated custom property moves the content inward so nothing gets clipped

You can also use it as a full-screen desk clock on a spare iPad or monitor, or as a Mac desktop widget.

Show me what you make: design a tile in the Studio, press Share and drop your link in the comments. Or build something with it, like a dashboard, a wall display or a widget for your site. Forks, new languages and PRs are all welcome.

Feedback very welcome, especially anything that feels off.

articles.title: How to Implement Spaced Repetition (SM-2) in JavaScript
articles.description: I spent a weekend convinced I could write a better review scheduler than the one Piotr Wozniak...
articles.body_html:
I spent a weekend convinced I could write a better review scheduler than the one Piotr Wozniak published in 1987. I couldn't. What I ended up with was a cleaner understanding of SM-2, the algorithm behind SuperMemo and, for most of its life, Anki. If you're adding any kind of "review this later" feature to an app, it's the place to start.

This post walks through SM-2 in plain JavaScript, points out the parts that trip people up, and covers what I'd change before shipping it to real users.

The idea in one paragraph

Hermann Ebbinghaus measured his own forgetting in the 1880s and found that memory drops fast after you learn something, then levels off. Each time you successfully recall it, the drop gets slower. Spaced repetition takes advantage of that: review an item right before you'd forget it, and push the next review further out every time you get it right. SM-2 is a small set of rules for deciding how far out "further" is.

What each card needs to store

Every item you schedule carries three numbers:

  • repetitions: how many times in a row it's been recalled correctly
  • interval: days until the next review
  • easeFactor: how quickly the interval grows, starting at 2.5

Plus a due date, which you calculate from the interval.

After each review the user grades their recall from 0 to 5. In the original paper 5 means perfect recall, 3 means correct but hard, and anything below 3 counts as a failure.

The code 

function sm2(card, quality) {
  let { repetitions, interval, easeFactor } = card;

  if (quality >= 3) {
    if (repetitions === 0) {
      interval = 1;
    } else if (repetitions === 1) {
      interval = 6;
    } else {
      interval = Math.round(interval * easeFactor);
    }
    repetitions += 1;
  } else {
    repetitions = 0;
    interval = 1;
  }

  easeFactor =
    easeFactor + (0.1 - (5 - quality) * (0.08 + (5 - quality) * 0.02));
  if (easeFactor < 1.3) easeFactor = 1.3;

  const due = new Date();
  due.setDate(due.getDate() + interval);

  return { repetitions, interval, easeFactor, due };
}

const fresh = { repetitions: 0, interval: 0, easeFactor: 2.5 };
let card = sm2(fresh, 4); // due tomorrow
card = sm2(card, 4);      // due in 6 days
card = sm2(card, 5);      // due in about 15 days

That's the whole algorithm. Twenty-odd lines.

The ease factor formula, decoded

The ease update looks like line noise, so plug in numbers. A grade of 5 adds 0.1. A grade of 4 adds nothing. A 3 subtracts 0.14. A 0 subtracts 0.8, though the floor of 1.3 stops it from going lower than that.

So a card you keep finding hard grows its interval slowly, around 1.3x per review at worst. A card you always nail grows faster and faster. The 1.3 floor matters more than it looks. Without it, a card you failed a few times would end up with an ease near zero and get shown to you every day forever.

Three things that bite you in production

Grades. Nobody wants six buttons. Anki settled on four (Again, Hard, Good, Easy), and most apps go even simpler. If you map "Again / Good / Easy" onto 1 / 4 / 5, the algorithm still behaves sensibly. I'd avoid letting users pick 0 through 5 directly. They'll use 3 and 5 and nothing in between.

Late reviews. SM-2 assumes people review on the due date. They don't. If a card was due 10 days ago and the user still remembers it, that's a stronger signal than an on-time success, but plain SM-2 ignores it. A common patch is to compute the next interval from the actual days elapsed instead of the scheduled interval when the answer is correct. Small change, much better behaviour for people who go on holiday.

Timezones. I set due with setDate above to keep the demo short. In a real app, store due dates as calendar days in the user's timezone, or someone in Kolkata will get tomorrow's cards at 5:30 in the morning and wonder what broke. I've shipped that bug. It's embarrassing.

Is SM-2 still worth using?

For a side project or an MVP, yes. It's predictable, it's easy to debug, and you can explain it to a user in two sentences.

It isn't state of the art anymore, though. Anki added FSRS (Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler) as an option in version 23.10. It fits a memory model to each user's actual review history instead of using fixed constants. If your app ends up with lots of review data per user, FSRS is worth a look. If you're starting from zero data, SM-2 gets you shipping this week.

The harder problem sits upstream of the scheduler

The scheduler turned out to be the easy part. The hard part was deciding what to put on the card in the first place.

Most of what I want to remember doesn't arrive as flashcards. It comes from a YouTube talk, a podcast episode, a long article, a reel someone sent me. Turning a 40-minute video into three or four reviewable ideas is real work, and most people (me included) never do it. So the videos sit in Watch Later and the scheduler has nothing to schedule.

That's the gap Recl is built around. You save videos, reels, podcasts or articles, it summarizes them, sorts them into topics, and then uses spaced repetition to bring the key points back before they fade. The scheduling logic is the same family of ideas as the code above. The difference is that the cards come from what you already consume, so you don't have to write them yourself.


A saved article turned into a short summary card in Recl's feed.

If you're building something similar, my advice is to spend less time tuning the interval math and more time on getting content into the system with as little friction as possible. A perfect scheduler with an empty queue helps nobody.

Try it yourself

Copy the function above, make a dozen cards from something you read this week, and grade yourself honestly for two weeks. You'll get a feel for the intervals faster than from any paper. And if you'd rather the cards wrote themselves from the stuff you save, give Recl a try.

I'm Spartan Rich, and I build Recl, an AI learning app that turns saved videos, podcasts and articles into summaries and spaced-repetition reviews.

articles.title: I scanned 100 apps built with Lovable. 14 were already dead. 1 leaked a live API key.
articles.description: I build Vespez (vespez.com), a tool that checks web apps for security and GDPR issues. I wanted a...
articles.body_html:
I build Vespez (vespez.com), a tool that checks web apps for security and GDPR issues. I wanted a real answer to a question I kept asking myself: AI tools make it trivial to ship an app, do they make it trivial to ship a safe one?

So I pulled 100 apps from Lovable’s own public showcase and ran every one through the same scan Vespez runs on any site: a headless browser loads the page, records what fires before the visitor clicks “accept” on consent, checks the response headers, and reads the privacy policy if one exists.

The numbers

100 apps checked. 14 were already offline within weeks of being shown off publicly. 86 got a full score.

Average security score: 77/100. Average GDPR score: 38/100.

One app was leaking a live OpenAI API key in its public JavaScript bundle, readable by anyone who opened dev tools. Not naming it, that gets reported privately, not broadcast.

What showed up constantly

96% have no Content-Security-Policy header. 92% can be embedded by another site (clickjacking). These travel together, 92% are missing both at once. That’s not 92 separate decisions, it’s a platform default: Lovable doesn’t set these headers for you, so unless someone specifically knows to add them, they just don’t exist.

55% load Google Fonts straight from Google’s servers. Same story, template default, not a deliberate choice, and also exactly the kind of third-party data flow GDPR actually cares about.

57% have no findable privacy policy. 63% have no terms of service. This part actually is on the builder, not the platform.

The cleanest result in the whole set: whether a consent banner existed was almost perfectly predictive of behavior. Apps with one loaded trackers before consent only 10% of the time. Apps without one did it 96% of the time. When the banner exists, it works. The gap is that 23 of 86 never added one.

Zero of the 86 scored a clean GDPR sheet. Three had zero security findings.

A smaller pattern worth a mention

Split by domain: apps still on a lovable.app subdomain averaged a GDPR score of 44. Apps that moved to their own custom domain averaged 34, worse, not better. Small sample (36 vs 50), so I’d call it a pattern worth watching rather than a law, but it’s a real one: moving to your own domain is usually a sign you’re treating it as a real product, which makes the gaps matter more.

Method, so you can judge it yourself

I took 100 apps from Lovable’s public showcase, via each project’s own “Visit website” link.

Each app got one scan: headless browser render, response headers, network requests and cookies recorded before any consent interaction, and privacy/terms pages read when findable.

Security findings are deterministic checks against the page and headers. For GDPR findings, where a privacy policy exists, an AI model reads it and checks what it says against what the site actually does.

Nothing from the pages was kept beyond scores and findings, same policy as real Vespez accounts.

14 apps were unreachable and excluded from the scores above.

Not a legal audit, a scan. Low score = likely issue, not a confirmed violation. Sample is a public AI-builder showcase, not a random slice of the web.

Curious if anyone’s seen similar patterns scanning their own AI-generated output, or if I’m missing an angle on the methodology.
